q: A payment API checks the caller token when a session starts but trusts the same session for every later request, even after an administrator revokes the user's permissions. Which design principle is being violated?
opts: Complete mediation, because every access must be checked each time it occurs
Separation of duties, because one user is performing the whole operation
Economy of mechanism, because the token check has too many steps
Open design, because the revocation logic is not publicly documented
why: Complete mediation requires that every access to every object be authorized at the time of the access, so a revoked permission takes effect immediately. A one-time check followed by cached trust breaks that. Separation of duties is about splitting a sensitive process among people, open design is about not relying on secrecy of the design, and economy of mechanism is about keeping mechanisms simple, none of which describes cached authorization.

q: A microservice that reads product images runs under a database administrator account because that was the quickest way to get it working. Which principle most directly calls for changing this?
opts: Defense in depth, by adding a second administrator account as a backup
Psychological acceptability, by making the account easier to remember
Least privilege, giving the service only the access it needs
Separation of privilege, by requiring two administrators to approve each query
why: Least privilege says each component should hold only the permissions required for its job, which here is read access to one data set. An administrator account lets any bug in the service become a full database compromise. Adding another administrator account, easier credentials or approvals per query do not reduce the excess privilege itself.

q: After a failed deployment, a gateway starts allowing all traffic through because its policy file could not be loaded. Which principle was ignored?
opts: Least common mechanism: policy files should never be shared between components
Open design: the format of the policy file must be published publicly
Accountability: every failed deployment must generate a signed audit record
Fail-safe defaults: access should be denied when the system fails or errors
why: Fail-safe defaults means that when something goes wrong, the system should end up in a secure state, normally denying access, and permission should be explicitly granted. A gateway that opens up when its policy fails does the reverse. Least common mechanism, open design and accountability are real principles but do not address the failure behavior in this scenario.

q: A team keeps its encryption algorithm secret and treats that as its main protection. A reviewer objects. What is the best basis for the objection?
opts: Security should rest on protecting keys, so a public, peer-reviewed algorithm is preferred
Secret algorithms are prohibited by nearly all data protection regulations in force today
A secret algorithm is fine as long as the keys are at least 256 bits long
Algorithms that are kept secret always execute more slowly than published algorithms do
why: The open design principle, which comes from Kerckhoffs, holds that a system should stay secure even if everything except the key is public, because secrets about design eventually leak and unreviewed algorithms often hide weaknesses. The other statements are not true: secrecy is generally legal, speed is unrelated, and a long key does not make a secret design safe.

q: A web form needs a security control against automated account takeover but users are already abandoning it because the rules are complicated. Which principle supports the best recommendation?
opts: Psychological acceptability: a protective control that people can use correctly
Economy of mechanism: remove the control entirely to cut down the complexity
Fail-safe defaults: block every login until the user proves identity in person
Defense in depth: require each user to pass every possible control available
why: Controls that are too hard to use get bypassed or abandoned, so the design should achieve the security goal in a usable way, for example with multi-factor authentication that fits normal workflow. Removing the control gives up the protection, blocking all logins breaks the service, and stacking every control makes usability worse.

q: An application stores a customer record worth about 40,000 dollars. An analyst estimates a successful attack would expose 25 percent of its value and happens twice every ten years. What is the annualized loss expectancy?
opts: 10,000 dollars
20,000 dollars
2,000 dollars
8,000 dollars
why: Single loss expectancy is 40,000 times 25 percent, which is 10,000 dollars. The annualized rate of occurrence is twice in ten years, or 0.2 per year. Multiplying gives 2,000 dollars per year. A countermeasure costing more than that annually would not be justified on this risk alone.

q: The product owner decides not to fix a moderate vulnerability in a legacy report module this quarter after reading the risk summary and signing a record of the decision. Which risk treatment is this?
opts: Risk acceptance, a knowing decision by the accountable owner
Risk avoidance, because the risk is no longer discussed
Risk mitigation, because the owner reviewed the vulnerability
Risk transference, because responsibility moved to the product owner
why: Acceptance means the accountable owner, informed of the risk, chooses to tolerate it, and it should be documented and revisited. Transference shifts financial impact to another party such as an insurer, avoidance eliminates the risky activity, and mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact with a control. Reviewing the issue is not itself mitigation.

q: Management wants a feature that would collect customers' contact lists even though the product does not use them. Applying privacy by design, what should the architect recommend FIRST?
opts: Do not collect the contact lists unless a documented purpose requires them
Collect them and arrange for staff to delete them manually after one year
Collect them and encrypt the stored copy with a strong, current algorithm
Collect them and display a detailed privacy notice on the sign-up screen
why: Privacy by design starts with data minimization: data that is never collected cannot leak or be misused, and each collected item needs a defined purpose. Encryption, notices and manual deletion are all weaker than not collecting unnecessary data in the first place.

q: A vendor ships a product with administrator remote access enabled and a default password, and relies on a hardening guide to tell customers to change it. Which concept does this contradict?
opts: Risk transference: the customer now owns all of the product risk
Secure by default: the product should ship already hardened
Non-repudiation: actions on the product cannot be tied to a specific person
Accountability: the vendor failed to publish the product access logs
why: Secure by default means the out-of-the-box configuration is already safe, so customers do not need extra steps to get protection. Shipping an insecure default and documenting the fix moves the burden to the customer. Non-repudiation and accountability are about tracing actions, and transference is a risk treatment, none of which fits.

q: A threat is described as an attacker with stolen credentials, and a weakness is described as the absence of multi-factor authentication. What is the risk?
opts: The stolen credentials themselves, since they are the asset that has been exposed here
The absence of multi-factor authentication, since it is the only item the team controls
The identity of the attacker, since risk is defined by who is carrying out the attack
The chance and impact of the attacker using the credentials against the gap
why: Risk is the combination of the likelihood that a threat exploits a vulnerability and the resulting impact. The threat is the attacker, the vulnerability is the missing control, and the credentials are an asset or an attack input. Treating any single element as the risk skips the likelihood and impact analysis.

q: Which TWO principles are both violated when a web service runs as an administrator and also skips authorization checks on internal calls because the caller is on the internal network? (Choose two.)
opts: Economy of mechanism
Least privilege
Complete mediation
Open design
Psychological acceptability
why: Running with administrator rights gives the service more access than it needs, which violates least privilege, and trusting internal callers without checking each access violates complete mediation. Psychological acceptability concerns usability, open design concerns secrecy of the design, and economy of mechanism concerns simplicity, none of which are described.

q: Which TWO statements about risk treatment are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Accepting a risk should be a documented decision by an accountable owner who understands the exposure
Mitigating a risk eliminates the threat completely
Avoiding a risk means installing a control that reduces its likelihood
Accepting a risk is the default outcome when no one responds to a finding
Transferring risk, such as through insurance or a contract, shifts financial impact but not the accountability for the decision
why: Transfer moves some financial consequence to another party while the organization remains accountable, and acceptance is only valid when an informed owner decides and records it. Avoidance means stopping the risky activity rather than adding a control, mitigation reduces but does not eliminate risk, and inaction is not an informed acceptance.

q: An application that has successfully authenticated a user has therefore authorized that user to perform any action the application offers.
opts: True
False
why: Authentication establishes identity only; authorization is a separate decision about what that identity may do, and it must be checked for each request according to the user's permissions.

q: Defense in depth means layering independent controls so that the failure of one control does not by itself expose the asset.
opts: True
False
why: Independent layers, such as input validation, authorization, encryption and monitoring, mean one failure is not enough for compromise. The layers must not share the same weakness or they add little.

q: Encrypting a message with a symmetric key that two parties share provides non-repudiation of who sent it.
opts: True
False
why: Either holder of the shared key could have produced the message, so neither can be proven to have sent it. Non-repudiation requires something unique to one party, such as an asymmetric digital signature, plus trustworthy logging.

q: Separation of privilege means that a sensitive action should require more than one condition to be satisfied before it is allowed.
opts: True
False
why: Instead of relying on a single check, the design requires several independent conditions, such as a valid session plus a second approval or factor, so one stolen credential or one bug is not enough. It is related to separation of duties, which splits a process across people, but it is a different principle.

q: A company's root signing key can only be activated when any two of five custodians each enter a share of the secret. Which security concepts does this arrangement combine?
opts: Defense in depth, achieved by using different vendors for each custodian share
Least privilege, achieved by reducing the run-time privileges of the signing service
Separation of duties, enforced through multi-party control with secret sharing
Complete mediation, achieved by re-checking the key on every signing request
why: Requiring several people to act together, with the secret split so that no one holds it all, is multi-party control and secret sharing, a technical form of separation of duties. Diverse vendors would be technical diversity, reducing run-time privileges is least privilege, and rechecking authority on each request is complete mediation, none of which describes the custodian arrangement.

q: A database is replicated to a second site in near real time. A faulty release corrupts many rows and the corruption reaches the replica within seconds. What does this show about replication?
opts: It protects integrity because the replica compares itself with the primary and rolls the change back
It protects availability but copies integrity damage, so point-in-time backups are still needed
It makes backups unnecessary because two live copies already exist at independent sites
It works only when clustering is also used to vote on which copy holds the correct values
why: Replication keeps copies in step, which helps when a node or site fails, but it faithfully copies bad writes and deletions as well. Recovering from corruption needs backups or versioned storage. Replicas do not automatically roll back changes, two live copies are not a substitute for backups, and clustering is not required to make replication copy changes.

q: An application advertises multi-factor authentication, but it asks for a password and then a security question answer. What is the best assessment?
opts: It is true multi-factor authentication because two separate prompts are shown
It is biometric authentication because the answer is personal to the user
It is two-factor authentication as long as the answer is stored as a salted hash
It is single-factor authentication used twice, because both are something the user knows
why: Multi-factor authentication needs factors from different categories, such as knowledge, possession and inherence. A password and a security question are both knowledge factors, so they add little. The number of prompts does not matter, a personal answer is not a biometric measurement, and how the answer is stored does not change its factor type.

q: A purchasing system must let auditors show that a named manager approved each large order and cannot later deny it. Which design is the most appropriate?
opts: Each approver signs the approval with a private key, and entries go into a tamper-evident log
Each approval is protected with a shared HMAC key that all managers use
Approval records are encrypted in the database with a strong symmetric algorithm
Approvers sign in with a password, and session logs stay editable by database staff
why: Non-repudiation needs something unique to the individual, such as an asymmetric digital signature, plus a log that cannot be quietly altered. A shared key means any holder could have produced the approval, encryption provides confidentiality rather than attribution, and logs that administrators can edit cannot be trusted as proof.

q: A product passed its annual compliance audit, yet a penetration test then finds exploitable flaws. Which statement best explains the difference?
opts: The penetration test must be wrong because passing the audit proves the software is secure
Compliance frameworks only cover availability, so security flaws are outside their scope
Penetration tests report only theoretical issues, so the findings can be set aside
The audit shows controls existed at a point in time, not current resilience
why: Governance, risk and compliance work shows that obligations are met, but compliance is a baseline measured at a point in time and does not guarantee the software withstands today's attacks. Audits do not prove security, frameworks are not limited to availability, and exploitable findings are not theoretical.

q: A payment service depends on a single authentication server, and every login fails when it goes down. Which change best applies the resiliency principle without weakening security?
opts: Add redundant authentication nodes with failover that still denies on failure
Let users continue with their last session while the server is unavailable
Raise the authentication server timeout so that it can wait longer for a response
Cache successful passwords in each client so logins can be verified locally
why: Resiliency removes the single point of failure with redundancy and failover, while the fail-secure default means a failure never grants access. Allowing unauthenticated continuation, caching passwords on clients or merely waiting longer either weaken authentication or leave the single point of failure in place.

q: Which TWO measures make defense-in-depth layers more independent of one another? (Choose two.)
opts: Spread critical services across geographically separate sites
Use different technologies or vendors for different protective layers
Host all layers on the same virtualization host to ease monitoring
Run every layer under one shared service account for simpler administration
Standardize on a single product for every layer to cut licensing costs
why: Technical diversity means one flaw in one product cannot defeat every layer, and geographic diversity means one site disaster does not take everything. Sharing an account, a host or a product creates a common point of failure that defeats independence even though it is simpler to run.

q: Split knowledge means that two people must act together to complete an operation, which is the same as dual control.
opts: True
False
why: Split knowledge means no single person knows the whole secret, for example each custodian knows half of a key. Dual control means two people must act together to perform an operation. They are related ways of enforcing separation of duties, but they are not the same, and answer choices often swap them.

q: A biometric template that has leaked can simply be reset, in the same way as a password.
opts: True
False
why: Biometric characteristics such as fingerprints cannot be changed, so a leaked template cannot be reissued, and matching is probabilistic with false accept and false reject rates. This is why biometrics are usually combined with another factor and the templates are protected carefully.

q: Meeting every regulatory requirement is sufficient evidence that a software product is secure.
opts: True
False
why: Compliance shows that required controls and processes exist, usually at a point in time. Threats change faster than regulations, so compliance is a baseline rather than proof of security.

q: Over several years an employee moves through four roles and keeps the access rights granted in each. An access review finds the employee can now both create and approve payments. Which problem and which control apply?
opts: Privilege creep, addressed by entitlement review and removal on role change
Fail-safe defaults, addressed by denying the employee all access for a trial period
Open design, addressed by publishing the list of who holds each entitlement
Economy of mechanism, addressed by merging all four roles into one broader role
why: Entitlements accumulate unless they are reviewed and removed when duties change, and the combination here also breaks separation of duties. Blanket denial, publication and a merged broader role either overreact or enlarge the access.

q: A company replaces eleven separate application logins and a spreadsheet of passwords with single sign-on and a password vault. Which design principle does this most directly serve?
opts: Least common mechanism, because users now share one login across the applications
Economy of mechanism, by using one small, well-reviewed mechanism rather than many
Open design, because the vault design is available to any employee who asks
Complete mediation, because the login now occurs only once per day
why: Consolidating authentication into one proven component reduces complexity and the number of places to get it wrong, which is economy of mechanism and a form of component reuse. The statement about sharing a login would actually describe a tension with least common mechanism, and a single daily check does not satisfy mediation.

q: Multi-tenant software keeps each customer's data in a separate schema, runs each customer's batch jobs in isolated containers and uses an allow list for the internal addresses that services may call. Which principle is mainly applied?
opts: Fail-safe defaults, because every call is blocked when the service is idle
Psychological acceptability, because the customers see no differences between tenants
Least common mechanism, using compartmentalization and isolation instead of shared resources
Defense in depth, because the schemas and containers are the same layer of control
why: Limiting what tenants share reduces leakage paths and limits the effect of one tenant failure, and allow lists restrict reachable destinations. The other principles are not what the isolation and allow list achieve.

q: An application records every approval in an append-only, blockchain-style ledger whose entries are chained by hash and signed by each approver. Which two properties does this primarily support?
opts: Availability and scalability
Confidentiality and data minimization
Non-repudiation and accountability
Authentication and single sign-on
why: Signed, hash-linked entries make it hard to deny or rewrite an action and give an audit trail that can be traced to the person. A ledger does not itself provide secrecy or capacity, and signing entries is not the same as logging in.

q: Which TWO changes would improve availability without weakening integrity or confidentiality? (Choose two.)
opts: Turn off input validation to reduce processing time per request
Run the service in a cluster across separate failure domains with automatic failover
Replicate the production database to a public test site for easy access
Add horizontal scaling that adds instances when demand rises
why: Redundancy, clustering, failover and elastic scaling support availability. Copying production data to a public site breaks confidentiality, and disabling validation reduces integrity protection.

q: Passwordless authentication with a phishing-resistant authenticator can improve both security and psychological acceptability.
opts: True
False
why: Removing memorized secrets reduces phishing and reuse, and sign-in becomes simpler for users, so people are less tempted to work around the control.

q: A company wants to compare its software security program with others in the same industry by looking at the activities those organizations actually perform. Which model fits BEST?
opts: BSIMM, because it describes what real programs are observed doing
CMMI, because it measures only hardware manufacturing quality
SAMM, because it prescribes the target activities for every organization
The Microsoft SDL, because it was written for Windows products only
why: BSIMM is a descriptive measurement of what many organizations actually do, which makes benchmarking against peers possible. SAMM and the SDL are prescriptive, telling you what to do rather than reporting what peers do. CMMI is a general process maturity model, not tied to hardware manufacturing, and the SDL is not limited to Windows.

q: A security lead wants a roadmap with measurable maturity levels across governance, design, implementation, verification and operations, tailored to the company's risk. Which framework is the BEST fit?
opts: STRIDE, which classifies threats against the elements of a system design
Common Criteria, which assigns evaluation assurance levels to evaluated products
OWASP SAMM, which defines five business functions with three maturity levels
NIST SP 800-61, which gives incident response recommendations
why: SAMM is organized into five business functions (governance, design, implementation, verification, operations), each with security practices and maturity levels, designed for building an improvement roadmap. SP 800-61 is incident response, Common Criteria evaluates products, and STRIDE is a threat classification model.

q: A federal customer asks a software supplier to attest that it follows secure development practices. The practices are grouped as prepare the organization, protect the software, produce well-secured software and respond to vulnerabilities. Which document is the customer referencing?
opts: The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, level 2
The NIST Secure Software Development Framework, SP 800-218
The BSIMM report for the supplier industry sector
NIST SP 800-53, the catalog of security and privacy controls
why: The SSDF organizes practices into exactly those four groups and is the basis of US federal secure software attestations. ASVS lists verification requirements for applications, BSIMM is a descriptive study, and SP 800-53 is a control catalog for systems rather than a development practice framework.

q: A team is moving from quarterly releases to deploying several times a day. Which approach to security activities is BEST?
opts: Automate checks in the pipeline and add security criteria to every story
Keep a single manual security review before the annual external audit
Freeze deployments until every developer completes a security certification
Move all security testing to a separate team that works after release
why: Frequent delivery needs security that scales with it: automated static analysis, dependency checks and policy gates in the pipeline plus testable acceptance criteria in each story. Periodic reviews and post-release testing cannot keep pace, and a blanket freeze would stop delivery without fixing the process.

q: A project manager asks what a security champions program contributes to the lifecycle. What is the BEST answer?
opts: A mandatory audit role that is independent of each development team
A group that holds the authority to approve or block every release
Embedded developers who promote secure practice and act as local contacts
A replacement for the central security team in smaller organizations
why: Champions extend security knowledge and early detection into each team and give the security team a scaled network of contacts. They are not an approval authority, they do not replace specialists, and they are embedded rather than independent auditors.

q: Which security metric BEST shows whether the vulnerability handling process is improving over time?
opts: The total number of vulnerabilities that one scanner reported this month
The count of lines of code scanned by static analysis each week
The number of developers who finished the annual training video
The trend in mean time to remediate vulnerabilities, by severity
why: A trend in time to remediate by severity shows how effectively the organization responds to findings. A raw count can rise because testing improved, training completion measures activity rather than outcome, and lines scanned says nothing about whether findings are fixed.

q: A high-severity change to a payment module must go live tonight to stop active fraud. What is the BEST way to handle change management?
opts: Wait for the next scheduled change board meeting in two weeks' time
Let the developer who wrote the fix deploy it without keeping any record
Bypass change management completely because the fix is so urgent
Use the emergency change path with delegated approval and review it later
why: Mature change management has an expedited path for emergencies that keeps accountability: delegated approval, a record and a retrospective review. Skipping the process leaves no control, waiting two weeks ignores the urgency, and an unrecorded single-person change breaks separation of duties.

q: A document says all production systems must use approved encryption. Another says AES-256 must be used for data at rest in the customer database. A third suggests developers consider hardware modules where practical. Which are correctly labeled in order?
opts: Procedure, standard, policy
Guideline, policy, standard
Standard, guideline, policy
Policy, standard, guideline
why: A policy is a high-level mandatory statement of intent, a standard is a mandatory and specific requirement such as a particular algorithm, and a guideline is optional recommended advice. A procedure would be the step-by-step instructions, which none of the three statements is.

q: Which TWO of the following are prescriptive frameworks that tell an organization what secure development activities to adopt? (Choose two.)
opts: CVSS
BSIMM
NIST SSDF
OWASP SAMM
SPDX
why: SAMM and the SSDF prescribe practices and, in SAMM, maturity levels to aim for. BSIMM is descriptive and reports what other organizations do, CVSS scores vulnerability severity, and SPDX is a format for software inventories.

q: Which TWO actions BEST adapt a secure SDLC to a fast agile and DevOps delivery model? (Choose two.)
opts: Move security requirements into a document that is not updated
Require a signed paper approval from the board before every sprint
Add security acceptance criteria to the definition of done for each story
Embed automated static analysis and dependency scanning in the pipeline
Perform one manual penetration test at the end of the project
why: Automated checks and testable acceptance criteria scale with fast iteration and provide continuous feedback. A single end-of-project test, per-sprint board approval and a static requirements document either arrive too late or are impractical at that speed.

q: The NIST SSDF describes secure development outcomes to achieve and can be used with any software development lifecycle model.
opts: True
False
why: The SSDF is a set of high-level practices grouped as prepare, protect, produce and respond. It states what to achieve rather than prescribing a step-by-step methodology, so it fits waterfall, agile or DevOps.

q: Finding and fixing a security defect during requirements or design is generally far cheaper than fixing it after release.
opts: True
False
why: The cost to correct a defect grows as it moves through the lifecycle, because more work depends on it and deployed fixes require patching and customer disruption. This is the rationale for shifting security left.

q: A security gate that any project manager can routinely waive without recorded justification still provides strong assurance.
opts: True
False
why: A gate only has value when it has clear criteria and a controlled exception process. Routine, unrecorded waivers mean nobody is actually accountable for the residual risk.

q: A security impact analysis is needed only for changes that are labeled as security fixes.
opts: True
False
why: Any change to requirements, code or environments can add or remove a control, so every change request is assessed for security impact, including feature changes and emergency changes, which are documented and reviewed afterward.

q: A pipeline fails builds that contain critical static analysis findings, but a release manager keeps lowering the threshold whenever a deadline approaches. What is the right approach?
opts: Remove the build gate and rely on a final manual review of the release
Let the release manager adjust the threshold since the manager owns the schedule
Raise the threshold permanently so the build never fails near a deadline
Set break/build criteria in advance; exceptions go to a named risk owner
why: A gate has value only when criteria are set beforehand and exceptions are controlled and recorded by the accountable risk owner. Removing it loses the control, giving the schedule owner the power to move the threshold defeats it, and a permanently raised threshold is simply a weaker control.

q: Which statement is the best example of an objective and key result (OKR) for a software security program?
opts: All third-party components must be approved by the architecture board
Lower dependency risk: fix 95 percent of critical flaws in 14 days
A weekly report listing every open vulnerability by application name
A scanner configured to run on every merge request in the repository
why: An OKR pairs a goal with measurable results for a period, here fewer exposed dependency flaws and a target fix rate. A mandatory approval rule is a policy, a weekly listing is a report and a scanner schedule is a tool setting, none of which states a measurable outcome.

q: A legacy portal is being retired. Which approach to data disposition is the most appropriate?
opts: Destroy all data immediately to remove risk, then ask legal what had to be kept
Archive every record indefinitely in case it proves useful to the business later
Check retention duties, archive what is needed, then destroy and record
Leave the data in place and simply cancel the licenses for the retired portal
why: Disposition follows retention rules: confirm what must be kept, archive it, securely destroy the remainder and document the destruction. Destroying first can break legal obligations, keeping everything forever increases breach exposure and violates privacy limits, and leaving data on a retired system leaves unmanaged risk.

q: A company learns on Monday that personal data of EU residents was exposed. By when must the supervisory authority be told under GDPR, where feasible?
opts: Within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach
Within 30 days after the forensic investigation is completed
Within 60 calendar days of the discovery date
At the next scheduled annual compliance audit
why: GDPR requires notification to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware. The 60-day figure belongs to the US HIPAA Breach Notification Rule, and waiting for a completed investigation or an annual audit would miss the deadline.

q: After the control assessment of a high-impact system, who should grant the authorization to operate?
opts: The senior official accountable for business risk
The lead developer, who knows the system better than anyone
The independent assessor who tested the controls
The security champion embedded in the development team
why: Authorization is a risk-acceptance decision made on the assessment evidence by someone with authority over the business or mission risk. Developers and security champions are not independent and lack that authority, and the assessor provides the evidence but does not accept the risk.

q: A team confirmed through reviews and traceability that the software matches its signed specification, yet users say it does not solve their real problem. Which activity would have exposed this?
opts: Additional static analysis of the source code
A larger penetration test of the deployed system
Validation with representative users
Raising the code coverage target for unit tests
why: Verification checks that the product was built right against its specification, and validation checks that the right product was built for real needs. Static analysis, penetration tests and coverage all assess correctness or security against the existing specification and cannot show that the specification itself was wrong.

q: A scanner reports a critical SQL injection in an isolated internal tool used by three staff with no sensitive data, and a medium flaw in the checkout flow. Management asks what to fix first. What is the best approach?
opts: Always fix the highest technical severity first, whatever it protects
Fix the checkout issue only, since internal tools never matter to the business
Translate each finding into business risk and let the owner decide
Defer both until the next annual penetration test confirms them
why: Technical risk describes the flaw, business risk describes what it means to the organization, and priorities and acceptance belong to those accountable for the business risk. Sorting only by technical score ignores context, declaring internal tools unimportant is an unjustified assumption, and waiting for an annual test leaves known issues untreated.

q: Which TWO are sources of secure development guidance referenced when adopting standards and frameworks? (Choose two.)
opts: The CVSS specification
SAFECode fundamental practices for secure software development
ISO/IEC 27034 application security guidance
The CAPTCHA specification
The SPDX specification
why: SAFECode publishes practical secure development guidance and ISO/IEC 27034 covers application security processes. CVSS scores vulnerability severity, SPDX describes software bill of materials data and CAPTCHA is a human-versus-bot challenge, so none of those is development guidance.

q: A single annual awareness video satisfies the need for role-based security training for developers, architects and operators.
opts: True
False
why: Different roles need different skills, such as secure coding for developers, threat modeling for architects and hardening for operators. Awareness raises general behavior, whereas role-based training builds specific skills and must be refreshed.

q: Under the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule, affected individuals must be notified without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery of the breach.
opts: True
False
why: That is the outer limit in the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule, with discovery starting the clock. GDPR is stricter for the regulator notification at 72 hours, and US state laws can add their own deadlines.

q: Verification confirms that the software meets the real needs of its users, while validation confirms that it matches its written specification.
opts: True
False
why: The definitions are reversed. Verification asks whether the product was built right against its specification and requirements, and validation asks whether the right product was built for real user needs.

q: A new compliance manager asks which security documents the project should produce and maintain. Which collection is most appropriate?
opts: Marketing plans, sales forecasts, office layouts and travel policies
Requirements, threat model, review and test records, risk acceptances
A single page stating that the software follows industry best practice
Only the final penetration test report, kept by the testing firm
why: Security documentation records decisions and evidence across the lifecycle so that others can build, verify, operate and audit the software. A slogan, unrelated business papers or a single report do not.

q: A program tracks the number of vulnerabilities found each month, and the number rose after the team adopted better scanners. How should the metric be interpreted and improved?
opts: The rise proves the developers are getting worse, so the scanners should be removed
The count is useless, so metrics should not be used to manage the program
The count may reflect better detection, so add trends like time to remediate
The count should be hidden from management to avoid unnecessary concern
why: Metrics must be interpreted in context and paired with outcome measures such as time to fix, criticality distribution and recurring weakness types, and tied to objectives and key results. Removing tools, abandoning measurement and hiding data remove insight.

q: An application is being retired at the end of its life. The credentials, DNS records and API keys it used are still active, and a license subscription renews automatically. Which decommissioning activities were missed?
opts: Threat modeling and misuse case writing for the retired application
Fuzzing and regression testing of the released build
Tokenization and obfuscation of the stored data
Credential and configuration removal, and license cancellation
why: End-of-life policies include removing credentials and configuration, cancelling licenses, archiving and meeting service level obligations, so no active access paths or costs remain. The other items are development-time activities.

q: A security lead wants a dashboard for executives and a separate feedback loop for developers. Which design best meets both needs?
opts: Executives see risk trends, and developers get findings in their tools
Both audiences receive the same weekly spreadsheet of raw scanner output
Executives receive nothing, and developers get a quarterly report
Developers see the dashboard, and executives read the commit logs directly
why: Reporting is tailored to its audience: summarized risk for decision makers and actionable detail for the people who fix the problems, with feedback to improve processes. Raw output, no reporting and swapped audiences are ineffective.

q: The business owner argues that a technical weakness in a back-office module is acceptable because it affects no revenue. The architect responds that the weakness allows access to the payroll database. What is the best way to frame the decision?
opts: Overrule the owner, since technical risk is always greater than business risk
Express the technical risk in business impact terms for the owner
Accept the owner's view, since business risk alone drives every decision
Remove the module from the risk register until it is exploited
why: Technical risk becomes a business decision when its consequence is stated in business terms, and the accountable owner then accepts, mitigates or transfers it. Overruling, ignoring technical risk and deleting the entry skip proper risk management.

q: A team following an agile method works in two-week sprints. Which approach best integrates security compared with a phase-gated waterfall method?
opts: Embed security tasks in every sprint, with acceptance criteria
Run one large security phase after the last sprint is complete
Skip security until the product backlog is empty
Hand all security work to a separate team that never meets the developers
why: In agile and DevOps the security goals do not change, but activities are scheduled in short cycles and automated, while waterfall maps them to phase gates. End-loaded or isolated security does not match the cadence.

q: A change to an authentication service has passed unit tests and is ready for production. The change board needs to include the Assessment and Authorization process. What does this process contribute?
opts: Control assessment and formal risk acceptance by an official
A rewrite of the code by the assessors to remove any defects found
A guarantee, issued by the vendor, that the system has no vulnerabilities
An automatic approval whenever all unit tests pass
why: Assessment tests the controls and authorization is the risk acceptance decision made on that evidence, repeated when the system changes. Assessors do not rewrite code, no one can guarantee no vulnerabilities, and passing tests is not authorization.

q: Which activity is an example of validation rather than verification?
opts: Letting representative users try the system in their real environment
Tracing each requirement to a design element and a passing test case
Reviewing the design and code against the signed specification
Running static analysis against the organization's coding standard
why: Validation asks whether the right product was built, which only real users in a real setting can confirm. Tracing requirements to tests, reviewing a design against a specification and checking code against a standard all verify that the product was built right against something written down.

q: An organization wants a software security standard for application security processes that auditors can assess, and a separate reference for payment software. Which pair fits?
opts: OWASP Top 10 and the CVSS scoring specification
SPDX and CycloneDX as machine-readable inventory formats
ISO/IEC 27034 and the PCI Software Security Framework
STRIDE and DREAD as threat modeling aids
why: ISO/IEC 27034 covers application security and the PCI Software Security Framework covers payment software. The other pairs are an awareness list and a scoring system, two SBOM formats, and two threat modeling aids.

q: Which TWO are appropriate inputs when defining the security metrics and reporting for a software program? (Choose two.)
opts: Criticality levels of applications, so results can be weighted by business importance
The total number of lines of code written by the team
The number of meetings held about security each quarter
Objectives that link measures to program goals, such as fixing critical findings within a set time
why: Metrics should connect to objectives and take criticality into account. Meeting counts and code volume measure activity, not security outcomes.

q: Decommissioning an application requires attention to data disposition, including retention duties, destruction and dependencies on the data.
opts: True
False
why: Retired systems still hold data subject to retention and privacy rules, and other systems may depend on it, so archiving or destruction must be planned and recorded.

q: Technical risk and business risk are the same thing, so the same people always make both decisions.
opts: True
False
why: Technical risk describes weaknesses and threats in the system, while business risk describes the consequences for the organization, and accountable business owners make the risk acceptance decisions informed by technical analysis.

q: A requirements document lists detailed features but says nothing about authentication, logging or data protection. What should the secure software professional do FIRST?
opts: Wait for penetration testing to show which controls turn out to be missing
Copy the control list from another team without checking whether it applies
Record the missing controls as defects to be fixed during integration testing
Elicit security requirements from data classes, laws and abuse cases
why: Security requirements must be defined early so they can be designed, built and tested, and they come from the data classification, applicable regulations, risk and abuse cases. Waiting for testing or treating them as defects makes fixes costly, and copying controls without analysis may miss real needs or add unneeded ones.

q: Which artifact BEST shows that each security requirement has been designed, implemented and tested?
opts: A ranked list of the penetration test findings, sorted by severity and component
A security requirements traceability matrix linking requirements to design and tests
A copy of the organization information security policy approved by management
A diagram of the production network topology showing every firewall and subnet
why: A traceability matrix maps each requirement to the design elements, implementation and test cases that satisfy it, exposing gaps in coverage. Findings, policy copies and network diagrams do not tie each requirement to its verification.

q: A designer wants to find security requirements by thinking like an attacker who abuses the checkout feature. Which technique does this describe?
opts: Creating a business impact analysis
Writing abuse or misuse cases
Calculating the annualized loss expectancy
Writing use cases for the intended user flows
why: Abuse and misuse cases describe how an attacker or careless user could subvert a feature and give rise to requirements such as rate limits, validation and lockout. Use cases cover intended behavior, ALE is a quantitative risk figure, and a business impact analysis identifies critical functions and recovery needs.

q: A hospital application stores diagnoses, billing addresses and appointment times. The architect needs a basis for deciding the encryption, access control and retention rules for each field. What should be done FIRST?
opts: Classify the data by sensitivity and regulatory scope together with the data owner
Ask the developers to decide which fields happen to be easiest to protect
Select the strongest available encryption algorithm and apply it to every field
Move all of the data to the cloud provider's default storage tier immediately
why: Classification by the data owner determines sensitivity and applicable rules, which then drive control choices. Applying the strongest encryption everywhere ignores context and cost, a default storage tier does not address requirements, and convenience is not a basis for protection.

q: A product will process personal data of people in the European Union for a new purpose. Which activity should happen during requirements, before design is finalized?
opts: A data protection impact assessment of risks to the individuals concerned
A load test that confirms response time targets are met under peak demand
A disaster recovery drill performed at the secondary site over a weekend
A code review focused on the layout and styling of the user interface
why: A data protection impact assessment is required under GDPR for high-risk processing and should shape requirements and design before data is collected. Load tests, interface reviews and recovery drills are valuable, but they do not assess privacy risk to individuals.

q: A sprint story states that the system must be secure. How can the team make this testable?
opts: Split it into two smaller stories without defining any further criteria
Move it to the project risk register where it will be recorded as an assumption
Replace it with measurable criteria, such as server-side validation of all inputs
Leave it as written and rely on the testers to judge whether it is satisfied
why: A requirement can only be verified if it has specific, observable criteria, so security stories need concrete acceptance conditions that become test cases. Judgement-based testing, burying it in a register and splitting it without criteria all leave it unverifiable.

q: The business states that after an outage it can tolerate no more than 15 minutes of lost transactions and must be running within two hours. How should this be recorded?
opts: An RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of two hours
An RTO of 15 minutes and an RPO of two hours
A generic availability figure of 99 percent without any time values
An ALE of 15 minutes and an SLE of two hours
why: Recovery point objective is the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time, here 15 minutes, and recovery time objective is the maximum time to restore service, here two hours. Reversing them is a frequent error. ALE and SLE are loss figures in money, and a generic percentage does not capture these targets.

q: A system holds low-impact public data, but a failure in its integrity could cause loss of life in a connected process. How does FIPS 199 categorize the overall system?
opts: Moderate, because the category is the average of the three impact ratings
Undetermined, because categorization must wait for a penetration test to finish
Low, because the data is public and confidentiality is the main property here
High, because the highest impact among the three properties sets the category
why: FIPS 199 uses the high-water mark, so a single high-impact property raises the system to high. Averaging or choosing only confidentiality understates the risk, and categorization is a design-time analysis that does not wait for testing.

q: An organization wants to verify web application security requirements at different assurance levels depending on risk, from basic to highly sensitive. Which resource is the BEST source?
opts: The OWASP Top 10, which is a ranked awareness list of web application risks
The SPDX standard, which describes formats for software component inventories
The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, which defines three levels
The CVSS specification, which scores the severity of individual vulnerabilities
why: ASVS provides detailed testable requirements organized into three levels for different assurance needs. The Top 10 is for awareness and is not a verification standard, CVSS rates findings, and SPDX describes bill of materials formats.

q: Customer data is retained indefinitely in an application because nobody defined a retention period. What is the MAIN risk this creates?
opts: Higher licensing costs for the database engine that holds the records
Reduced mathematical accuracy of the encryption algorithm in use
Larger breach impact, and possible violation of laws that limit retention
A noticeably longer response time for the application login function
why: Keeping personal data longer than needed enlarges what an attacker can steal and can breach laws requiring deletion once the purpose ends. Licensing cost, encryption accuracy and login speed are not the main security concern.

q: Which TWO factors should drive the security requirements for an application that stores health records of patients in several countries? (Choose two.)
opts: The data classification and sensitivity of the records
The brand guidelines for the user interface
The privacy and health laws that apply to those patients
The release date requested by the sales team
The preferred programming language of the team
why: Requirements come from what the data is and what laws and contracts govern it. Language preference, brand guidelines and release dates can influence implementation or scheduling but do not set the required security and privacy controls.

q: Which THREE items would normally be captured in logging requirements for an application? (Choose three.)
opts: Which security events must be recorded, such as login failures and privilege changes
That every character a user types must be recorded in plain text for later debugging
That developers may edit log entries afterward to correct mistakes
That passwords and full payment card numbers must never be written to logs
How long logs must be retained and how they are protected from tampering
why: Good logging requirements say what to log, how long to keep it and how to protect it, and exclude sensitive data. Recording everything users type creates a privacy and security hazard and editable logs defeat accountability.

q: Which TWO are valid sources of abuse and misuse cases? (Choose two.)
opts: Outputs of threat modeling for the same feature
The firmware version of the build server
The monthly cloud billing report
Brainstorming with stakeholders about how an attacker would subvert a feature
why: Abuse cases come from adversarial thinking and structured threat analysis of the feature. Billing reports and build server firmware have no direct connection to how a feature could be abused.

q: Security requirements are best identified early in the lifecycle, because requirements that are never stated are rarely designed, built or tested.
opts: True
False
why: Requirements drive design and testing. A control that is not specified is easily missed and expensive to add later.

q: Under GDPR, consent is the only lawful basis on which personal data may be processed.
opts: True
False
why: GDPR lists six lawful bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests. Which one applies depends on the processing, and the requirements should record it for each purpose.

q: PCI DSS is an industry standard enforced through contracts with card brands and acquirers rather than a law, but non-compliance can still lead to fines and loss of card processing.
opts: True
False
why: PCI DSS is set by the payment card industry and applied through contract, unlike statutes such as GDPR or HIPAA. The consequences are still real: fines passed on through the acquirer and the loss of the ability to process cards.

q: An RTO states how much data loss is tolerable, while an RPO states how long a restoration may take.
opts: True
False
why: The definitions are reversed. RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service and RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as a period of time.

q: A developer asks who decides how customer billing data should be classified. Who is correct?
opts: The database administrator who stores and backs up the data
The developer who implements the features that use the data
The cloud provider that hosts the database service
The business data owner who is accountable for the data
why: The data owner is the accountable business role that classifies data and approves access. Administrators and developers act as custodians who apply the owner's decisions, and a hosting provider does not decide how a customer classifies its own data.

q: Sensitive customer details have spread into spreadsheets, emails and shared folders. What should be done first to define handling requirements?
opts: Encrypt the main customer database column by column
Block email attachments across the whole organization
Move all shared folders to a lower-cost storage tier
Discover and classify the unstructured data first
why: Unstructured data has no schema, so it must be found and classified before rules can be applied. Encrypting the database does not touch the copies, blocking attachments is a blunt control with no classification basis, and moving storage tiers does not address handling requirements.

q: A team replaces customer names with random identifiers but keeps a mapping table so support staff can look people up. How is the resulting data treated under GDPR?
opts: It is pseudonymized and still personal data
It is anonymized and falls outside the regulation
It is aggregated data, which is exempt from the regulation
It is public data, because the names are no longer displayed
why: Because the mapping table can restore the link to the individual, the data is only pseudonymized and remains personal data with its protections. Anonymization requires that people cannot reasonably be re-identified. Replacing a name with an identifier does not make data aggregated or public.

q: A privacy requirement states that users can ask for their personal data to be deleted. Which design requirement best makes this achievable?
opts: Delete the person's data in every store, log and processor
Display a notice that deletion requests can be sent to the support mailbox
Mark the account as inactive and hide it from all screens
Encrypt the data and discard the user's password hash
why: Erasure works only if the system can find and remove a single person's data everywhere it lives, including copies and processors, while recording lawful reasons to keep some of it. A notice, hiding the account or discarding a hash leaves the personal data in place.

q: A software-as-a-service product serves EU and US customers, and EU customers require that their data stays in the EU. Which requirement best expresses this?
opts: All traffic uses TLS and the data may be stored in any region
EU tenant data, keys, backups and support access are pinned to EU regions
The terms of service say that data may be moved to any region
Every tenant is replicated to all regions to maximize availability
why: Data residency is an architecture requirement that must cover storage, keys, backups and even administrative access. Encrypting traffic does not control location, terms of service cannot override the customer requirement and replicating everywhere breaks it.

q: An audit finds service accounts from a finished project that still have database access. Which missing requirement is the root cause?
opts: Longer and more complex passwords for all service accounts
Multi-factor authentication for batch jobs run by service accounts
Named owners and periodic reapproval with removal at project end
A shared service account for all batch jobs in the company
why: Access that nobody reapproves only accumulates, so provisioning requirements need ownership, scope, periodic recertification and deprovisioning at the end. Stronger passwords or MFA do not remove access that should not exist, and a shared account would worsen accountability.

q: The architecture board mandates that all new services use one approved cryptographic library. Which source of compliance requirement is this?
opts: A regulatory authority requirement
A statutory legal requirement
An industry-specific requirement
A company-wide standard
why: Requirements that a company imposes on its own development tools, libraries, frameworks and protocols are company-wide standards. Regulatory, legal and industry-specific sources come from outside the company, from regulators, statutes and sector standards such as PCI.

q: Which TWO items belong in the security requirements for an outsourced development vendor? (Choose two.)
opts: Notification of vulnerabilities and incidents within an agreed time
A requirement to brand dashboards with the vendor logo
Unlimited subcontracting without notice to the customer
The vendor's preferred code editor and window layout
A right to audit the vendor's secure development practices
why: Vendor requirements address how the supplier builds and handles security: timely notification and the ability to verify practices. Editor choice and logos are irrelevant, and unlimited unannounced subcontracting would remove control over who touches the code.

q: Data labels should travel with the data as metadata so that tools such as data loss prevention can apply the handling rules automatically.
opts: True
False
why: A label that exists only in a policy document cannot be enforced by systems. Attaching the classification to the data, for example as metadata or headers, lets storage, sharing and loss prevention tools act on it automatically.

q: A hardening baseline for the deployed system is normally written as a non-functional requirement.
opts: True
False
why: Non-functional requirements cover security, operational, continuity and deployment qualities. A required hardening baseline, supported platforms and installation privileges are deployment requirements and are tested like other requirements.

q: A story reads "As a customer I can reset my password", and another says "Password reset links must expire within 15 minutes and be single-use". How should these be classified?
opts: The first is functional, the second non-functional security
The first is non-functional, the second is a use case
Both are functional, because both concern the same feature of the system
Both are non-functional, because they mention passwords
why: Functional requirements say what the system does, and security, operational and continuity qualities are non-functional constraints. The expiry and single-use rule constrains how the feature must behave.

q: A defense contractor builds a patient scheduling tool for a hospital that takes card payments, using the contractor's approved libraries only. Which list covers the compliance requirement sources?
opts: Only the company's library standards, because they are the closest to the developers
Only the payment card industry standard, because it is the only one with fines
Health regulation, card industry standard, contract and company standards
The marketing requirements, because they define the customers and markets
why: Compliance comes from regulators, law, industry-specific obligations and company standards, and all that apply to the data and market must be identified. Single-source answers miss obligations.

q: A company labels documents Public, Internal, Confidential and Restricted, and attaches each label to the data as it is created. Which requirement does this support?
opts: Avoiding any need for access control, because the label alone stops disclosure
Eliminating the need for data retention rules, because labels apply forever
Removing the data owner role, because the system now classifies by itself
Consistent handling rules driven by sensitivity and impact
why: Labels make sensitivity visible to people and systems so rules apply consistently, but they do not enforce anything on their own and do not replace owners or retention rules.

q: E-mail addresses were collected only to send order receipts, and the marketing team now wants to use the same addresses for promotional campaigns. Which privacy requirement is most directly at issue?
opts: Data residency: the addresses must stay in the region where they were collected
Purpose limitation: reuse needs a new lawful basis such as consent
Data portability: customers must be able to export their addresses
Retention: the addresses must be deleted as soon as the receipt is sent
why: Purpose limitation means personal data is collected for a stated purpose and not reused for an incompatible one without a new lawful basis such as consent. Residency, portability and retention are real privacy topics, but none of them is triggered by this change of use.

q: A misuse case for a checkout feature describes an attacker replaying a discount code many times. Which element should the team add to complete it?
opts: A description of the colors used on the checkout page
A list of the developers who wrote the feature
The date by which the case will be removed from the backlog
Mitigating controls, such as single-use codes
why: A useful misuse case names how the abuse is prevented or detected, and the controls become requirements and tests. Presentation details, authorship and backlog dates do not.

q: Late in the project the product owner drops a security requirement for rate limiting. How does a security requirements traceability matrix help the team respond?
opts: It ranks the remaining requirements by CVSS score and attacker skill
It replaces the change approval for dropping the requirement
It shows which design elements, code and tests are linked to that requirement
It records which attackers could exploit the missing control
why: An SRTM links each requirement to its source, design, implementation and tests in both directions, so a change or removal shows which elements are affected. It does not rank requirements by CVSS, replace change approval or model attackers.

q: A company is outsourcing the development of a module to a contractor. When should vendor security requirements be defined?
opts: Before selection, in the requirements
After delivery, when the module is available to test
Only if the contractor asks for them
After the first security incident involving the module
why: Vendor requirements, such as secure development practices, vulnerability handling and audit rights, belong in the baseline before selection, and verifying them follows in the supply chain domain.

q: Which TWO are good examples of non-functional security requirements? (Choose two.)
opts: The user sees a confirmation page after ordering
The user can search products by name
The service must resume within two hours of a regional failure
All administrator actions must be logged and the logs retained for one year
why: Logging, retention and recovery targets are qualities and constraints on how the system behaves. Searching and confirmation pages are functional behaviors.

q: Which TWO belong in the data lifecycle requirements for personal data? (Choose two.)
opts: A policy that backups are exempt from every privacy rule
A secure and verifiable disposal method at the end of its life
A plan to keep all data forever as a source of future analysis
Rules for how long data is retained and where it is stored
why: Lifecycle requirements span collection, storage, use, sharing, retention and disposal. Keeping data forever and exempting backups violate retention and privacy principles.

q: Fully anonymized data that cannot reasonably be re-identified generally falls outside privacy regulations that apply to personal data.
opts: True
False
why: Anonymization removes identifiability, whereas pseudonymization does not. The determination depends on whether re-identification is reasonably possible, including by combining data sets.

q: A data dictionary is the document that records which users hold access to each data store.
opts: True
False
why: A data dictionary describes data elements, their meaning, format and sometimes classification. Access is recorded in access control lists, provisioning records and review reports.

q: A third-party processor that receives personal data from the application relieves the application owner of requirements for that data.
opts: True
False
why: The organization stays accountable for the data it shares and must flow down requirements and verify them, including for retention, deletion and security.

q: A team is asked to find what could go wrong in a new design, classifying threats as spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. Which method is it using?
opts: STRIDE
CVSS
DREAD
PASTA
why: STRIDE is the threat classification scheme named by those six categories. DREAD scores severity, PASTA is a seven-stage risk-centric process, and CVSS scores the severity of known vulnerabilities, so none of those is a classification of threat types.

q: After threats are identified, the team needs to rank them by damage potential, reproducibility, exploitability, affected users and discoverability. Which technique applies?
opts: STRIDE
DREAD
An attack tree
LINDDUN
why: DREAD rates threats using those five factors so the team can prioritize. STRIDE categorizes rather than ranks, LINDDUN is a privacy-focused threat method, and an attack tree models paths to an attacker goal.

q: An architect wants a threat modeling approach that begins with business objectives, defines technical scope, simulates attacks and ends with risk and countermeasure analysis. Which should be chosen?
opts: Trike, which excludes any attacker perspective
STRIDE, which analyzes each diagram element for six threat types
DREAD, which provides a scoring formula only
PASTA, a seven-stage risk-centric method
why: PASTA is risk-centric and attack-simulation based, linking technical threats to business impact through seven stages. STRIDE and DREAD are narrower, and Trike is a risk-based approach that does model threats against assets, so the claim that it excludes attackers is wrong.

q: During threat modeling on a data flow diagram, where should the team concentrate FIRST?
opts: On flows that cross trust boundaries, because data changes trust level there
On the user interface colors and layout, because users see them first
On the oldest components, because age alone indicates exposure
On flows entirely inside a single process, because they are the most numerous
why: Threats cluster where data passes between zones with different trust or privilege, such as from the internet into the application or from the application into the database. Internal flows, interface appearance and age are less reliable indicators of exposure.

q: A company uses a VPN so that any device on the internal network can reach the HR system without further checks. Which change best aligns with zero trust?
opts: Add a second perimeter firewall in front of the existing first one
Authorize every request using identity, device and context
Hide the HR system address from the internal DNS records
Extend the VPN so that contractors and partners can use it as well
why: Zero trust removes implicit trust from network location and evaluates every request against identity, device state and policy. Another firewall and a wider VPN keep the perimeter model, and hiding a DNS record is obscurity rather than an access decision.

q: A microservices system authenticates users at the API gateway, and internal services trust any call that reaches them. What is the MOST significant weakness?
opts: Anyone inside the network can call any service without being checked
Logs cannot be correlated across the different services at all
Individual services will not be able to scale horizontally under load
The gateway cannot terminate TLS connections coming from external users
why: If internal services trust all callers, a single compromised component or network foothold gives access to every service. Design should authenticate service identities (for example with mutual TLS) and authorize in each service. The other issues are unrelated to the trust model.

q: An API endpoint returns an order to a signed-in caller who supplies an order identifier. A tester signed in as one customer changes the identifier to another customer's order number and receives that order. Which API design flaw is this?
opts: Excessive rate limiting, which ended up exposing the order data
Broken object level authorization: ownership is never checked
Broken authentication, since the tester had no account at all
Insufficient logging, which causes the identifiers to be exposed
why: The caller is authenticated but the API does not verify the caller is allowed to access that specific object, which is object level authorization. Rate limiting does not expose data, the tester did have valid credentials in this scenario, and logging does not cause the data exposure.

q: A company moves a workload to a platform as a service offering. Which responsibility remains with the customer?
opts: Providing physical access control for the provider datacenters
Securing its own code, data, identities and configuration
Patching the underlying hypervisor and the physical hosts
Maintaining redundancy of the provider network backbone
why: In the shared responsibility model the provider manages the infrastructure and platform layers, while the customer is always responsible for their data, identities, access configuration and the code they deploy. Hypervisor patching, physical security and the backbone are provider responsibilities.

q: A team builds a container image for a customer-facing service. Which design choice BEST reduces risk?
opts: An image with credentials baked in so deployment needs no further configuration
A full operating system image that includes the debugging tools for convenience
An image that runs as root so that file permissions are simpler to manage
A minimal scanned image run as non-root, with secrets injected at runtime
why: Smaller images have fewer components to be vulnerable, scanning finds known flaws, non-root limits what a compromise can do, and runtime secrets keep credentials out of the image. Extra tools, root and embedded credentials each enlarge the attack surface or leak secrets.

q: A designer wants single sign-on across several applications and needs a protocol that carries the identity of the authenticated user on top of OAuth 2.0. Which is correct?
opts: OpenID Connect
Kerberos with a shared service account
Basic authentication over HTTPS
The OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow alone
why: OpenID Connect adds an identity layer, with an ID token about the authenticated user, over OAuth 2.0. OAuth 2.0 alone is for delegated authorization, not authentication, Kerberos with a shared account does not provide federated identity of this kind, and Basic authentication sends credentials with every request.

q: A design review finds that sensitive keys will be stored in the same database as the encrypted data they protect. What is the BEST recommendation?
opts: Hold keys in a separate key service or hardware module
Keep the keys where they are but raise the database backup frequency
Rename the key column so the keys are harder for an attacker to find
Encrypt the key using the same key to double the protection it provides
why: Separating key management from the data means an attacker who gets the data does not automatically get the means to decrypt it, and key services provide rotation, access control and audit. Renaming is obscurity, self-encryption is circular, and more backups would spread the keys further.

q: Which TWO are benefits of attack surface reduction? (Choose two.)
opts: Removal of the need for authentication on remaining features
A guarantee that no vulnerabilities remain
Fewer entry points that an attacker can probe
Automatic compliance with every regulation
Less code and configuration to maintain and defend
why: Removing unneeded features, ports and accounts shrinks what must be tested and defended. It does not guarantee a vulnerability-free product, it does not remove the need to authenticate the remaining functions, and compliance requires more than a smaller surface.

q: Which TWO design measures address threats of spoofing and elevation of privilege respectively? (Choose two.)
opts: Strong authentication, such as multi-factor authentication
Encrypting data at rest
Authorization checks that enforce least privilege on every request
Rate limiting on public endpoints
Digital signatures on log files
why: Spoofing is answered by authentication, and elevation of privilege by authorization with least privilege. Signing logs addresses tampering and repudiation, rate limiting addresses denial of service, and encryption at rest addresses information disclosure.

q: Which TWO are appropriate controls when designing a serverless function that processes events from a public queue? (Choose two.)
opts: Validate every event as untrusted input
Share one broad administrator role among all the functions
Give each function its own narrowly scoped identity
Embed secrets in the function source for speed
why: Event sources are inputs that attackers can influence and per-function identities with minimal permissions limit damage. A shared broad role and embedded secrets both violate least privilege and secrets handling.

q: An attack tree places the attacker's goal at the root and breaks it down into the alternative or combined steps that could achieve it.
opts: True
False
why: Branches joined by OR nodes are alternatives and branches joined by AND nodes must all succeed, often annotated with cost or probability, so the tree shows the cheapest or likeliest path. It starts from the attacker's goal, whereas a data flow diagram starts from the system and its components.

q: In a zero trust architecture, a request from a device inside the corporate network is trusted by default.
opts: True
False
why: Zero trust removes implicit trust based on network location. Each request is authenticated, authorized and evaluated using identity, device state and context.

q: SAML assertions let an identity provider tell an application who has been authenticated, which allows single sign-on across several applications.
opts: True
False
why: SAML is a federation protocol in which an identity provider issues signed assertions about the authenticated user to the applications that trust it. OpenID Connect plays a similar role on top of OAuth 2.0, which by itself only delegates authorization.

q: Because containers share the host kernel, they generally provide weaker isolation between workloads than separate virtual machines.
opts: True
False
why: A flaw in the shared kernel can affect every container on the host, so extra measures such as non-root users, restricted capabilities and network policies matter.

q: In an infrastructure as a service model, the customer is responsible for patching the guest operating system of the virtual machines it deploys.
opts: True
False
why: The provider secures the physical hosts, the network and the hypervisor, but everything from the guest operating system upward belongs to the customer, and data, identities and configuration always remain the customer's responsibility.

q: An enterprise architect wants a risk-driven framework that traces business requirements down to security services and controls, with views for the business, the architect, the designer and the builder. Which is the best fit?
opts: The Open Web Application Security Project Top 10 list of web risks
The Common Criteria assurance levels for evaluated products
The Sherwood Applied Business Security Architecture (SABSA)
The STRIDE method for categorizing threats on a data flow diagram
why: SABSA is a layered, business-driven security architecture method that derives controls from business requirements. The Top 10 is an awareness list, Common Criteria evaluates products against a Security Target, and STRIDE classifies threats rather than building an architecture.

q: A purchasing workflow passes a request through a web tier, an application service and a payment service. Each hop re-verifies the caller and propagates the original user identity, so the payment service can see who really initiated the request. Which pattern is this?
opts: Security chain of responsibility, where each link verifies and passes along the trust information
Single sign-on, where one login replaces the checks that every later service would otherwise make
Defense in depth through geographic diversity of the three tiers
Least common mechanism, where the tiers share one authentication component
why: In a chain of responsibility each component takes its turn deciding whether to accept or refuse, and passes trusted identity context on to the next.
