SSO is about reducing logins rather than skipping later checks, geographic diversity is about location, and sharing one component runs against least common mechanism.

q: A design uses a queue so a front-end service can hand work to back-end workers asynchronously. Which security concern is specific to message queuing?
opts: Messages may be read, forged or replayed unless the queue is secured
The queue guarantees ordering, which means producers no longer need to be authenticated
Asynchronous processing removes the need to validate the content of each message
A queue is internal infrastructure, so only the front-end service needs authorization
why: A broker is another trust boundary: anything that can publish may inject work, and anything that can read may disclose it, so access control, integrity and confidentiality of messages must be designed in. Ordering does not authenticate, consumers still validate untrusted payloads, and the broker itself must be access controlled.

q: An enterprise service bus connects dozens of legacy services through web services. A review recommends validating message schemas and signing messages at the bus. What is the main reason for centralizing this?
opts: Policy is enforced consistently at one chokepoint, not re-implemented per service
The bus becomes a trusted component, so backend services can drop their own authorization
Signed messages remove the need for transport encryption between any two services
Schema validation at the bus makes each service safe from injection in its own code
why: A central enforcement point gives consistent policy and a place to log, but it does not replace defense in depth: services still authorize and validate. Message signatures give integrity and origin, not confidentiality, and bus validation does not remove injection flaws inside a service.

q: A rich internet application downloads a large script bundle and performs most business logic in the browser, calling back-end APIs. Which design decision is most important?
opts: Obfuscate the script bundle so that users cannot see which API endpoints exist
Treat the client as untrusted and enforce authorization on the server
Move the validation rules into the client so that the server does less work
Check permissions once when the application loads and cache the result in the browser
why: Anything running on the user's device can be inspected and altered, so the server must remain the authority for access decisions and input checking. Obfuscation is not a control boundary, client-only validation is bypassed by calling the API directly, and a cached permission breaks complete mediation.

q: A smart building system uses thousands of low-power sensors that report over a wireless mesh to a gateway. The vendor can reach them only for rare firmware updates. Which design choice best addresses the long-lived, unattended nature of these devices?
opts: Signed firmware updates verified by the device, with secure boot
A single shared password burned into every sensor at the factory for easy support
Disabling encryption on the wireless mesh so the low-power chips last longer
An open maintenance port on each sensor so technicians can patch it quickly
why: Devices that cannot be touched often need an authenticated, tamper-resistant update path, trust anchored in hardware, and unique credentials so one compromise does not unlock the fleet. A shared password, no encryption and an open port each remove a control that the environment makes hard to restore later.

q: A set-top device must refuse to run any firmware that was not published by the manufacturer. Which embedded security mechanism provides this?
opts: Secure boot, where each stage verifies a digital signature on the next before running it
Secure memory, which encrypts the working memory used by applications
A watchdog timer that resets the device if software stops responding
Address space layout randomization, which varies the location of code in memory
why: Secure boot starts from an immutable root of trust and checks the signature on each stage, so unsigned or altered firmware does not run. Secure memory protects data, a watchdog helps availability, and ASLR makes memory exploitation harder after code is already running.

q: A company is replatforming an application from its data center to a software as a service product for a non-core function. Compared with running the software itself, which design responsibility remains with the customer?
opts: Patching the operating system of the hosts that run the service
Configuring identities, access and data protection settings
Applying application code fixes for vulnerabilities in the vendor product
Securing the physical facilities and the network behind the provider service
why: In SaaS the provider runs the infrastructure and the application, so the customer keeps responsibility for user access, configuration and the data it stores there. Host patching, product code fixes and facilities all belong to the provider.

q: A fitness application quietly uploads the phone contact list, location history and device identifiers to an analytics vendor, although none of it is needed for the features. Which design concern does this illustrate?
opts: Insufficient obfuscation of the mobile binary, which exposes the analytics code
Weak session handling between the mobile client and its API gateway
Implicit data collection that conflicts with data minimization
Excessive logging on the device, which fills the storage of the phone
why: Mobile apps and embedded SDKs often collect data the user never knowingly provided, which is a privacy requirement problem as much as a security one. The scenario describes collection and sharing, not binary protection, sessions or device logging.

q: Two virtual machines from different tenants share a physical processor. A researcher shows that timing differences in the cache can reveal secrets from one to the other. Which statement best describes the mitigation approach?
opts: Apply microcode and operating system updates, and isolate sensitive workloads
Add input validation to the application, which closes the cache timing channel
Encrypt all network traffic between the tenants so the timing cannot be observed
Increase the memory allocated to the virtual machines so caches are not shared
why: Side-channel and speculative execution weaknesses are hardware-level and are reduced through firmware and OS mitigations, careful isolation and sometimes dedicated hardware. Input validation, network encryption and more memory do not touch a processor cache channel.

q: A design team is adding a model-driven assistant to a support portal. The assistant can read tickets and call internal tools to reset passwords. What is the best design decision?
opts: Trust the assistant output because it was trained on the company's own data
Give the assistant an administrator identity so that it can complete any request
Treat model output as untrusted and limit the tools it can call
Rely on a prompt that tells the model never to reveal anything confidential
why: Models can be manipulated through the content they read, so the output that drives actions needs the same controls as any untrusted input, plus least-privilege tool access and approval for risky operations. Trusting training data, over-privileging the identity or relying on an instruction in a prompt each leave the control to the thing being attacked.

q: A hospital buys an infusion pump that will stay in service for fifteen years, and a security patch may require clinical safety testing before release. Which design stance best fits this industrial and medical IoT context?
opts: Apply every patch automatically on release, because confidentiality always outranks availability
Place the pump on the general office network so it can be monitored with standard tools
Prioritize safety, segment the device and plan a validated update process
Accept the lack of updates because medical devices are not worth attacking
why: Operational and medical devices live for years and a failure can hurt people, so designs lean on segmentation, limited exposure and a controlled, tested update process. Automatic patching can itself create safety risk, mixing the device into the office network adds exposure, and assuming nobody will attack is not a risk decision.

q: Administrators manage a payment platform from the same network and credentials used for ordinary customer traffic. Which change best addresses the design of the management interface?
opts: Keep the interface where it is and rename the administration URL
Allow administration only during office hours but leave it on the shared network
Move administration to an isolated management network with its own auditing
Share one administrator account among the team so everyone can respond quickly
why: Management and log interfaces are high-value targets and belong behind separate, tightly controlled paths, which is the idea behind out-of-band management. Renaming a URL is obscurity, time limits do not reduce exposure, and a shared account destroys accountability.

q: Application A passes customer records to application B every night, and the two share a long-lived symmetric key kept in a configuration file on both servers. Which interface design improvement is most important?
opts: Keep the file but double the key length so that the key is harder to guess
Move the key into the source code of both applications for easier deployment
Use per-application credentials, a key service and key rotation
Send the key by email to each new administrator so access is not lost
why: Keys and data shared between applications are a dependency whose protection must be designed: unique credentials, controlled storage, rotation and minimal data. A longer key in the same file adds little, and source code or email are weaker places than a key service.

q: A design uses data loss prevention (DLP) at the email gateway and on endpoints. Which limitation should the designer keep in mind?
opts: It stops all data leaving the organization once it is switched on
It depends on detection rules, so evasion and false positives remain
It replaces the need for data classification because it inspects every file
It protects data at rest in databases, so access control is no longer needed
why: DLP is a detective and preventive control that relies on knowing what sensitive data looks like and on seeing the channel. It does not guarantee prevention, it works best with classification rather than instead of it, and it does not replace access control.

q: A server uses a Trusted Platform Module. A designer wants the application to release a disk encryption key only when the machine booted with the expected firmware and operating system. Which TPM capability supports this?
opts: Random number generation to produce a stronger password for the administrator
Hosting the application code so that it runs faster than on the main processor
Acting as a firewall that filters traffic before it reaches the network card
Measured boot with sealing the key to platform configuration values
why: A TPM can record boot measurements in platform configuration registers and seal secrets so they are released only when those measurements match, which ties the key to a known state. It is not an accelerator or a firewall, and random numbers alone do not bind a key to the boot state.

q: A reporting team needs access to customer data in a production database, but only to some columns. Which database design technique best limits what they can see while keeping the data in one place?
opts: Give them the database owner account and ask them to avoid the other columns
Copy the whole table into a spreadsheet and send it to the team by email
Give access through a view or column-level privileges
Create a trigger that deletes the sensitive columns after each report runs
why: Views and fine-grained privileges let the database itself enforce which columns a role can read, which is least privilege at the data layer. Asking people to avoid columns is not enforcement, exporting copies spreads the data, and a trigger that deletes columns destroys data.

q: An architect has to pick between defending a single large data store with one strong control or applying layered controls to the same store. The data is highly sensitive. Which approach reflects the secure design principles best?
opts: Use the strongest possible encryption alone, because it makes the other controls redundant
Layer independent controls: segmentation, authorization, encryption and monitoring
Place the store inside the perimeter and trust all internal systems to reach it freely
Hide the database server name from the application documentation to reduce discovery
why: Defense in depth assumes any single control can fail, so independent layers are chosen for the most sensitive assets. A single control, implicit internal trust and hiding names each depend on one assumption holding.

q: Which activity is the best example of selecting reusable technology for credential management in a new application suite?
opts: Using the enterprise identity provider with SSO and managed certificates
Letting each application keep its own user table with a different hashing scheme
Building a custom token format so that attackers cannot recognize it
Storing all passwords in one spreadsheet shared with the support desk
why: Reusing a proven identity provider and managed PKI centralizes policy, auditing and rotation, and follows economy of mechanism and component reuse. Separate user tables, a home-made token and a shared spreadsheet multiply the places where credentials can leak.

q: A team is deciding where to run untrusted plug-in code written by customers. Which choice best limits the damage a malicious plug-in can do?
opts: Run the plug-ins inside the main application process so they start quickly
Run each plug-in in a sandbox with a restricted identity and resource limits
Review each plug-in manually once and then let it run with application privileges
Sign the plug-ins with the vendor key and trust them from that point onward
why: Isolation with reduced privileges and quotas contains a bad plug-in even when review misses something. In-process execution gives full application access, a one-time review does not keep up with updates, and a signature shows origin rather than safety.

q: A threat modeling team wants a method that combines parts of other methods and adapts them to the organization and its software lifecycle, instead of adopting one named approach unchanged. What describes this?
opts: CVSS, which produces the list of threats for each design element automatically
DREAD, which both discovers threats and chooses the mitigations to apply
A hybrid method that blends techniques such as STRIDE and attack trees
A penetration test, which is the first step in every threat model
why: A hybrid method deliberately combines elements, for example identifying threats with STRIDE, modeling attack paths with trees and prioritizing with risk analysis. CVSS scores vulnerabilities that exist, DREAD only rates, and a penetration test needs an implemented system.

q: A design review lists threats from a competitor with a large budget who stays inside a network for months, a staff member with legitimate access, and a compromised software supplier. Which set of threat categories does this describe?
opts: Advanced persistent threat, insider threat and supplier threat
A denial of service attack, a phishing campaign and a zero-day exploit
A script kiddie, a hacktivist and a natural disaster
Spoofing, tampering and repudiation as defined in STRIDE
why: Long-term stealthy access by a resourced adversary is an APT, legitimate access abused is an insider threat, and a compromised vendor is a supply chain threat. The other lists mix actor types and technique categories that are not described in the scenario.

q: A threat model identified a credible attacker goal, but the team cannot say how likely it is or which techniques would be used. Which input would most improve the analysis?
opts: Threat intelligence on the actors and techniques targeting such systems
A longer list of generic threats copied from an unrelated industry
A larger penetration test budget to be spent after the design is complete
The CVSS base scores of vulnerabilities in the office printers
why: Threat intelligence helps pick credible, relevant threats and predict how they would be carried out, so effort goes where it matters. Generic lists, late testing and unrelated vulnerability scores do not describe the adversaries in question.

q: After a design review, the architect must rank two proposed mitigations. One costs little and removes an exposed administrative port; the other is expensive and addresses a threat with low impact. Which approach to prioritization is best?
opts: Always start with the most expensive control, because cost indicates protection
Choose by risk reduced for cost and effort, so the port removal comes first
Fund both equally so that no stakeholder objects to the allocation
Postpone both until a penetration test confirms which one matters
why: Controls are prioritized by the risk they reduce relative to their cost and dependencies, and removing an unneeded exposed port is cheap and high value. Price is not protection, even funding is not risk-based, and waiting for a test delays an obvious design fix.

q: A team wants to compare how well a candidate architecture meets a 99.95 percent availability target with how much latency encryption adds. Which design activity does this represent?
opts: Modeling non-functional security properties and constraints
Writing misuse cases for the login page after the first release
Running static analysis against a prototype to count coding defects
Cataloguing the open-source licenses in the dependency tree
why: Quantified non-functional properties, such as availability, latency and the cost of controls, are modeled in the design so conflicts surface early. The other options describe abuse case writing, code analysis and license review.

q: The deployment topology of a new service puts the continuous delivery system, the container registry and the production cluster in one flat network, all administered by one shared role. Which change best supports a secure operational architecture?
opts: Leave the topology as it is and add a banner warning staff to be careful
Segment the environments, separate roles and limit the pipeline access
Add a second shared role so one can serve as backup for the other
Move the registry to production so that images are close to where they run
why: A secure operational architecture limits blast radius through segmentation and separated, minimal roles for build, registry and runtime. A banner is not a control, another shared role keeps the problem, and putting the registry in production merges more trust zones.

q: An application caches the user role in a long-lived cookie it trusts without checking it again, to avoid database lookups. Which principle does the design violate, and what is the fix?
opts: Open design; publish the cookie format so that outsiders can review it
Complete mediation; check authorization on each request on the server
Least common mechanism; give every user a separate cookie name
Economy of mechanism; remove cookies and pass the role in the URL
why: Trusting a client-held value without verification means access is not mediated on each request, and the fix is server-side authoritative data or an integrity-protected short-lived token. Publishing the format, renaming cookies or moving the role into the URL do not restore the check.

q: Which TWO statements about secure interface and protocol design for an API are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Verbose error responses help clients and are safe to return in production
Responses should return only the fields that the caller is permitted to see
A stateless API does not need authentication because no session is stored
Using POST rather than GET makes a request secure against tampering
Authorization should be checked on the object and the function being requested, not only at the gateway
why: Object and function level authorization and minimal responses are core API controls. The HTTP method does not provide integrity, stateless APIs still authenticate every call (usually with a token), and verbose errors disclose internals.

q: Which TWO are appropriate for protecting data on a mobile application design? (Choose two.)
opts: Log full request bodies on the device so that support can troubleshoot problems
Disable certificate checks in production to avoid connection errors
Embed the API secret in the application package, since the package is signed
Validate server certificates on every network call and fail closed
Store tokens and keys in the platform keystore or keychain rather than in plain files
why: Hardware-backed storage and certificate validation are the standard mobile protections. A signed package can still be unpacked to reveal secrets, logs on the device may expose personal data, and disabling certificate validation allows interception.

q: Which THREE items belong in a threat model of a web application that uses a third-party payment service? (Choose three.)
opts: Threats against each element and flow, categorized for example with STRIDE
Mitigations, owners and a way to validate that they work
The office floor plan showing where developers sit
A data flow diagram with the trust boundary between the application and the payment service
A list of the favorite tools of the development team
why: A useful threat model scopes the system with trust boundaries, finds threats on each element and records what will be done and verified. Tool preferences and floor plans are not threat analysis.

q: In a service-oriented architecture, a security token that the enterprise service bus has validated may be trusted by every downstream service without any further checking.
opts: True
False
why: Each service remains responsible for authorization and validation of what it receives. Treating the bus as a universal trust anchor means one compromised component or token gives access to everything.

q: Replacing a firmware update path that checks signatures with one that accepts any file from the manufacturer web site makes a device easier to maintain without changing its security.
opts: True
False
why: Without signature verification, anyone who can alter the download or impersonate the site can install malicious firmware. Secure update depends on the device verifying authenticity and integrity before applying a change.

q: A hardware security module keeps cryptographic keys in tamper-resistant hardware, so applications can use the keys without being able to read them out.
opts: True
False
why: Keys are generated and used inside the module, which performs the cryptographic operations on request, so a compromised application or administrator cannot simply copy the key material. Access to the module still needs strong authentication and auditing.

q: In a peer-to-peer design there is no central point of trust, so the application does not need to authenticate the other peers it exchanges data with.
opts: True
False
why: Peers can be malicious or impersonated, so identities and messages still need authentication and validation. Removing the central server removes a single point of failure, not the need for trust decisions.

q: Using augmented or virtual reality features in an application can raise privacy design concerns because sensors may capture the surroundings and biometric-like data of the user and bystanders.
opts: True
False
why: Cameras, depth sensors and motion tracking collect data about people and places, so purpose, consent, retention and protection must be designed in. This is part of the outline's attention to cognitive computing and immersive technologies.

q: A threat model that is completed once at the start of a project remains valid for the life of the software.
opts: True
False
why: Architecture, data flows and threats change, so the model should be updated when the design, technology or threat landscape changes and revisited during reviews.

q: A search page builds its database query by concatenating the search text into the SQL statement. Which fix is the MOST effective?
opts: Strip single quotes out of the input before it is concatenated
Show a generic message whenever the database query fails
Use parameterized queries so that input is always treated as data
Hide the search page behind a very long and unpredictable URL
why: Parameterization separates code and data so the database never interprets input as SQL syntax, which solves the problem at its root. Stripping quotes is a fragile block-list, an obscure URL provides no protection, and hiding errors does not stop injection.

q: A comment field echoes user input inside an HTML page, and a tester inserts script that runs in other users' browsers. Which control is the PRIMARY defense?
opts: Encrypting the database column that stores the comments
Context-aware output encoding when the data is rendered
Requiring all users to change their passwords more often
Raising the maximum length allowed for the comment field
why: Cross-site scripting is prevented chiefly by encoding output for its context so the browser treats it as text, with input validation and a content security policy as additional layers. Encryption at rest, a longer field and password rotation do not stop script execution in the browser.

q: A banking site relies on session cookies. An attacker lures a logged-in user to a page that silently submits a transfer request to the bank. Which defense directly addresses this?
opts: Hashing the session identifier in the database
Limiting the number of failed logins
Output encoding of the account number
Anti-forgery tokens plus SameSite cookies
why: Cross-site request forgery depends on the browser automatically attaching cookies, so a per-request unpredictable token and SameSite cookies defeat it. Output encoding is for script injection, hashing session identifiers protects them in storage, and login throttling targets guessing attacks.

q: A developer must store user passwords. Which approach is BEST?
opts: Hash each password with a unique salt using Argon2id or bcrypt
Store the passwords in plain text inside a well access-controlled database
Encrypt the passwords with AES so that they can be recovered when forgotten
Hash every password with plain SHA-256 and without any salt
why: Passwords never need to be recovered, so they should be hashed with a unique salt and a deliberately slow, memory-hard algorithm to make offline guessing expensive. Reversible encryption exposes all passwords if the key is taken, unsalted fast hashes are cracked quickly with tables and GPUs, and plain text is unacceptable.

q: A scan of the repository history shows a cloud access key committed six months ago and removed the next day. What should be done?
opts: Add a comment to the code warning developers never to commit any keys
Rewrite the repository history and carry on using the same key
Do nothing, since the key was removed from the current version of the code
Revoke and rotate the key, and adopt a secrets manager with scanning
why: Anything committed to version control may have been copied or cached, so the secret must be revoked and replaced regardless of deletion. A secrets manager and automated secret scanning address the root cause. Removing it from the current version or merely rewriting history cannot undo any copies, and a comment is not a control.

q: A C program copies user input into a 64-byte array with an unchecked function. Which long-term action BEST reduces this class of vulnerability?
opts: Use bounds checking and move the component to a memory-safe language
Enable verbose error messages so that overflows are easier to diagnose
Rely only on address space layout randomization to stop exploitation
Run the program only during off-peak hours when traffic is low
why: Bounds checking removes the bug, and memory-safe languages eliminate whole classes of memory errors. Randomization is a mitigation that raises the difficulty of exploitation without fixing the flaw, verbose errors leak information, and timing has no effect on exploitability.

q: An application checks that a file is writable by the user and then, in a separate step, opens it for writing. An attacker swaps the file for a link to a system file between the two steps. What flaw is this?
opts: A cross-site request forgery weakness
An insecure direct object reference in the URL
A buffer over-read in the file system driver
A time-of-check to time-of-use race condition
why: The state checked is not the state used because it changed between the check and the use, which is the definition of TOCTOU. Fixing it means performing the check and use atomically on the same handle. The other options describe different weakness categories.

q: A web application shows users a full stack trace and the database query when an error occurs. What is the BEST remediation?
opts: Remove logging from the application so that no details exist anywhere
Show the stack trace only to users who have logged in to the application
Encode the stack trace so that it is harder for a casual visitor to read
Show users a generic message and keep the details in protected logs
why: Detailed errors reveal internals useful to attackers, while developers still need diagnostics, so keep them in protected logs and give users a generic message. Showing traces to logged-in users still leaks to any account holder, encoding does not help, and removing logs destroys accountability.

q: A reviewer wants to find authorization logic flaws and design mistakes in a new module, not only pattern-based bugs. Which review approach is BEST?
opts: A spelling and style check of the comments and identifiers in the source code
A static analysis scan run with the default rule set and no further review
A vulnerability scan of the production network performed by the operations team
Manual secure review by an experienced reviewer, complemented by automated tools
why: Business logic and authorization flaws need human understanding of intent, and tools add breadth for known patterns, so a combination is strongest. A default scan misses logic flaws, a network vulnerability scan does not examine code logic, and comments are not security relevant.

q: A team wants to ensure no single compromised developer account can push malicious code to the main branch. Which control is MOST effective?
opts: A single shared team account that all of the developers log in with
Branch protection requiring an independent approved review, with signed commits
A weekly email asking developers to confirm that their commits are legitimate
Disabling the audit log in order to save repository storage space
why: Requiring independent review enforces separation of duties so one account cannot merge alone, and signed commits tie changes to identities. Shared accounts destroy accountability, an email confirmation is not an enforcement, and removing logs weakens detection.

q: A server component fetches any URL supplied by the user and returns the content. An attacker supplies an internal cloud metadata address and receives credentials. Which weakness is this?
opts: Cross-site scripting
SQL injection
Server-side request forgery
Session fixation
why: The server is tricked into making a request to a destination chosen by the attacker, reaching internal resources. Defenses include allow-listing destinations and blocking internal ranges. XSS targets browsers, SQL injection targets databases, and session fixation concerns session identifiers.

q: Which TWO measures together best prevent SQL injection and cross-site scripting in a web application? (Choose two.)
opts: Longer session timeouts
Context-aware output encoding when displaying data
Parameterized queries for database access
Hiding the server version banner
Disabling the audit log
why: Parameterization prevents data being interpreted as SQL and output encoding prevents data being interpreted as script. Session timeouts, disabled logging and banner hiding do not address either attack at its root.

q: Which TWO are correct practices for secrets management? (Choose two.)
opts: Keep secrets in environment-specific configuration files in the repository
Store secrets in a dedicated manager with access control, rotation and auditing
Share one service account password among all developers
Rotate any secret that has ever been committed to a repository
why: A secrets manager centralizes control and a leaked secret must be considered compromised. Committing configuration with secrets and sharing one password both create exposure and remove accountability.

q: Client-side input validation is sufficient to protect an application from malicious input, because the user interface will reject bad data.
opts: True
False
why: Attackers can bypass the client entirely and send requests directly, so validation must be enforced on the server. Client-side checks are a usability aid only.

q: Setting the HttpOnly attribute on a session cookie prevents scripts running in the page from reading it, which limits what cross-site scripting can steal.
opts: True
False
why: An HttpOnly cookie is not exposed to JavaScript, so injected script cannot copy the session identifier directly. It does not stop the script from acting as the user in the page or remove the cross-site scripting flaw, so output encoding is still the primary defense.

q: A unique random salt for each password defeats precomputed hash tables and makes identical passwords produce different stored hashes.
opts: True
False
why: Because the salt is combined with the password before hashing, an attacker cannot reuse one precomputed table against every account, and two users with the same password get different hashes. Salting does not make guessing slow, which is why a slow algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt is also needed.

q: For server-side request forgery, allow-listing the destinations a server may call is generally stronger than trying to block a list of internal addresses.
opts: True
False
why: Block lists miss alternative encodings, redirects and DNS tricks that still reach internal addresses, whereas an allow-list permits only destinations that are known to be needed. Blocking internal ranges and restricting egress are useful additional layers.

q: Hiding a link from the user interface is an adequate access control for an administrative function.
opts: True
False
why: Access control must be enforced on the server for each request. A hidden link can be found or guessed, and an unprotected endpoint can be called directly.

q: A framework lets developers protect a method either with an annotation such as a required role declared outside the code, or with an explicit permission check inside the method body. Which statement best contrasts the two styles?
opts: Declarative security is enforced only on the client, while programmatic security runs on the server
Programmatic security is always the weaker option because explicit checks are skipped by the runtime
Declarative security cannot be audited because the rules are not visible to anyone reading the code
Declarative rules sit outside the code, programmatic checks can use object data
why: Declarative rules, such as role annotations or deployment descriptors, are easy to review and change without editing code, whereas programmatic checks handle object-specific decisions such as whether this user owns this record. Both run on the server, and neither is inherently weaker.

q: Two requests withdraw money from the same account at the same moment. Each reads a balance of 100, checks that 80 is available, and both succeed, leaving the account overdrawn. Which fix is most appropriate?
opts: Show a generic error message when the balance changes between the two reads
Increase the database connection pool so that each request has its own connection
Add client-side validation that disables the button after the first click
Make the check and update atomic, with a transaction or version check
why: The flaw is a race condition, so the read, check and write must be one atomic operation or detect conflicting changes. Error messages, a bigger pool and a disabled button do not stop two server requests from interleaving.

q: A web service catches every exception, writes nothing to the log and returns a normal success response so that users never see errors. What is the main security problem?
opts: The success response reveals the exact version of the framework to the attacker
Catching exceptions is itself prohibited by every secure coding standard
Users will assume the system is faster than it really is under heavy load
Failures become invisible, so attacks and unsafe states go unnoticed
why: Handling exceptions is expected, but swallowing them silently hides attacks and can leave the transaction half done. The right pattern is a specific handler, a fail-secure outcome, a generic message to the user and a protected log entry.

q: A product displays user profile text inside an HTML attribute and inside a JavaScript block. A developer applies HTML body encoding in both places. Why is this not sufficient?
opts: Encoding must be applied before the data is stored, never when it is displayed
Attributes cannot be encoded safely, so user text must never be placed in them
Each context needs its own encoding, and HTML encoding fails in JavaScript
Encoding is only a usability feature and does not affect script execution
why: Output encoding is context-sensitive: body, attribute, JavaScript and URL contexts have different dangerous characters. Encoding on output for the specific context is the recommended defense, and attributes can be encoded safely.

q: A developer logs the entire login request, including the password field, so that support can diagnose failed logins. What is the best response during review?
opts: Accept the practice, because logs are stored on an internal server
Encrypt the log file but continue recording the passwords in it
Keep secrets and sensitive personal data out of logs, retaining context
Stop logging authentication events altogether so nothing sensitive is recorded
why: Logs support auditing and diagnosis but become a data store of their own, so credentials and sensitive personal data must be excluded or masked. Internal storage and encryption do not make recording passwords acceptable, and removing authentication logging loses accountability.

q: After users log in, a site continues to use the same session identifier that was supplied before authentication. An attacker plants a known identifier and waits. Which control prevents this?
opts: Lengthen the session identifier so it is harder to guess
Shorten the idle timeout from thirty minutes to fifteen minutes
Issue a new session identifier at login and invalidate the old one
Hash the session identifier before storing it on the server
why: The attack is session fixation, defeated by regenerating the identifier on authentication and privilege change. A longer identifier, a shorter timeout and storing a hash do not help when the attacker already knows the value the victim will keep using.

q: An application loads a plug-in over HTTP from a partner site, then calls its functions with full application privileges. Which implementation change best reflects handling of untrusted libraries and APIs?
opts: Keep the HTTP link but confirm that the partner site has a professional design
Get it from a verified source, check integrity and limit its privileges
Copy the code into the repository without review so it is under source control
Rely on the partner contract alone and skip technical checks on the component
why: Third-party code is untrusted until verified, so integrity checks, trusted provenance and minimal privileges contain the risk. A contract, a pleasant website or simply copying code into a repository do not verify the component or limit what it can do.

q: A service reads uploaded images into memory, without a size limit, and also keeps database connections open after errors. Under load it crashes and starves other applications. Which implementation practice is lacking?
opts: Output encoding on the image metadata returned to the browser
Tokenization of the file names that users choose when they upload
Resource management: limits, timeouts and reliable release
Digital signatures on every uploaded image before it is processed
why: Unbounded allocation and leaked handles let one actor exhaust compute, memory or connections, a resource-based denial of service. Limits, timeouts and release in finally blocks address it. Encoding, tokenization and signatures are not related to exhaustion.

q: A retailer must keep card numbers available to a fulfillment system but wants most of its applications to fall outside payment compliance scope. Which technique is the best fit?
opts: Base64 encoding of the card number before it is stored
Hashing the card number with a fast, unsalted algorithm
Tokenization, with the card number held only in a protected vault
Truncating the stored value to the last four digits and the expiry date
why: Replacing the number with a random surrogate means systems that handle only tokens never hold card data, which shrinks scope, while the vault is protected. Base64 gives no protection, a fast unsalted hash of a small number space is easy to reverse, and truncation cannot support later fulfillment.

q: A product team wants a runtime containment mechanism for a component that parses untrusted documents, so a parser exploit cannot reach the rest of the system. Which approach is most suitable?
opts: Run the parser in the main process but under a more descriptive thread name
Compile the parser with logging turned off to reduce its attack surface
Run the parser in a locked-down sandbox or container
Give the parser read access to the whole file system so it can find fonts
why: Isolation techniques such as sandboxes, containers and separation kernels limit what a compromised component can reach. Thread names, logging settings and broader file access do nothing to contain an exploit.

q: An application encrypts data with a cipher hard-coded in dozens of places. A weakness is announced, and the team estimates months to replace it. Which design property would have made this easier?
opts: A longer key length chosen for the original algorithm in advance
Cryptographic agility, with algorithms chosen through configuration
A decision to keep the cipher secret so that attackers could not study it
Disabling encryption for internal traffic so there is less to maintain
why: Crypto agility means the algorithm choice is isolated so it can be changed with limited effort when weaknesses appear or standards change, for example post-quantum transitions. Longer keys do not fix a broken algorithm, secrecy violates open design, and removing encryption removes the control.

q: A document system lets each file owner decide who can open the file, and a clearance label on users and files decides what no owner can override. Which pair of access control models does this describe?
opts: Role-based access control for owners, plus attribute-based access control for labels
Discretionary access control for owners, plus mandatory access control for the labels
Mandatory access control for owners, plus discretionary access control for labels
Rule-based access control for owners, plus identity-based access control for labels
why: DAC lets owners grant access at their discretion, while MAC enforces central label-based policy that users cannot change. The other pairs reverse the models or describe models that do not match owner-granted sharing and fixed labels.

q: A designer wants sensitive computation to stay protected even if the operating system or another process on the same host is compromised. Which category of control addresses this at the hardware level?
opts: Cross-site request forgery tokens attached to every form submission
Parameterized queries, which keep SQL code separate from user data
A password policy that requires symbols and a minimum length
Processor extensions such as memory encryption and enclaves
why: Microarchitecture extensions, for example trusted execution environments, memory encryption and pointer authentication, provide isolation that software alone cannot. CSRF tokens, parameterization and password rules operate at other layers.

q: A team wants to reuse an internal utility that has been copied between projects for years. Which action best supports secure code reuse?
opts: Move it into a maintained shared library with an owner and tests
Keep copying the source into each project so every team can tweak its own version
Rewrite it from scratch for each project to avoid inheriting old vulnerabilities
Mark it as approved because it has been in production for several years
why: A single owned, versioned and reviewed component can be fixed once and updated everywhere, which is the benefit of common controls and libraries. Copies drift and keep old flaws, rewrites reintroduce mistakes, and age is not evidence of safety.

q: A secure coding guide asks developers to avoid the weakness class recorded as CWE-79 and the one recorded as CWE-89. Which two weaknesses are these?
opts: Cross-site scripting and SQL injection
Buffer overflow and use after free
Cross-site request forgery and path traversal
Hard-coded credentials and missing authentication
why: CWE-79 is improper neutralization of input during web page generation (cross-site scripting) and CWE-89 is SQL injection. The other pairs are different weaknesses with their own identifiers.

q: A new maintainer pushes a change that contains a check for a specific date and then silently deletes records, and a commit that sends data to an unusual host when a particular user name is typed. Which kinds of malicious code do these illustrate?
opts: A race condition and a buffer overflow
A phishing kit and a keylogger
A worm and a rootkit
A logic bomb and a backdoor
why: Code that triggers destructive behavior on a condition such as a date is a logic bomb, and a hidden path activated by a special input is a backdoor. Detection relies on code review, behavior and integrity checks, and indicators such as high-entropy encoded blobs.

q: A reviewer finds a long block of high-entropy data in a source file and a routine that decodes and executes it at run time. What does this most likely indicate, and what is the next step?
opts: Possibly packed or hidden malicious code, so analyze it and trace who introduced it
A harmless compression technique, so the file can be approved as submitted
A cryptographic validation test vector, which should be stored with the tests
A formatting error that the linter will fix when it next runs
why: High entropy and run-time decoding are typical of obfuscated payloads, so the code should be examined, its origin investigated and the build quarantined if needed. Assuming it is benign or a lint issue ignores a recognized malicious code indicator.

q: A security team needs to detect unauthorized changes to the application binaries and configuration files on production hosts, and to restart the service automatically if it stops responding. Which pair of controls fits?
opts: Fuzzing and code coverage
Data loss prevention and tokenization
File integrity monitoring and a watchdog
Dependency pinning and software composition analysis
why: File integrity monitoring compares files against a known-good baseline, and a watchdog detects a hung service and restarts it. Fuzzing and coverage are test activities, DLP and tokenization protect data, and pinning and SCA address dependencies.

q: A static analysis scan finds a serious flaw in a legacy module that will be retired in six months, and fixing it needs a major rewrite. The product owner must choose a risk strategy. Which is the best documented decision?
opts: Ignore the finding, because the module will be retired anyway
Transfer the risk to the scanner vendor through the license agreement
Close the finding as a false positive so the dashboard stays clean
Mitigate, then record acceptance until the retirement date
why: Findings are addressed by a deliberate strategy: fix, mitigate, accept, transfer or avoid. Here mitigation plus a recorded acceptance with an end date is defensible. Ignoring a finding, transferring risk to a tool vendor or relabeling it as false positive are not legitimate treatments.

q: Two organizations connect their systems into a larger service, each assuming the other has already checked inputs. Which approach best addresses security in systems-of-systems integration?
opts: Agree trust contracts on what each side validates, then test together
Assume each system is secure because it passed its own acceptance test
Connect them first and rely on monitoring to reveal gaps later
Let the larger partner decide security rules without documenting them
why: Integration creates new trust boundaries, so responsibilities for validation, authentication and logging must be explicit and verified through joint testing and analysis. Separate acceptance tests do not cover the combined behavior, and undocumented rules cannot be tested.

q: A release build is created with compiler options that enable stack protection, position-independent code and warnings treated as errors. A developer wants to silence a warning about an unchecked buffer copy. What is the best action?
opts: Add a pragma that hides the warning in all builds going forward
Remove the warnings-as-errors option so the build passes
Fix the code that causes the warning, rather than suppressing it
Move the line into a third-party file so the warning is no longer reported
why: Compiler warnings often point to real defects, and security-relevant switches such as stack protection and ASLR support add defense in depth. Suppressing, relaxing or hiding the warning leaves the underlying flaw.

q: The build pipeline signs release binaries and a second step strips symbol names and renames internal classes. What do these two steps provide, respectively?
opts: Confidentiality of the code through signing, and integrity through obfuscation
Availability through signing, and non-repudiation through obfuscation
Access control through signing, and nonrepudiation of users through obfuscation
Origin and integrity from signing, and obscurity from obfuscation
why: Code signing lets recipients verify who released the code and that it was not changed, while obfuscation only makes analysis harder and is never a security boundary. The other pairings assign properties to the wrong techniques.

q: Which TWO are correct statements about input handling? (Choose two.)
opts: Sanitizing input once makes it safe for every later output context
Canonicalize input first, then validate it against an allow list on the server
Prefer rejecting invalid input over trying to repair it
Validation in the browser is enough if the form uses a modern framework
Block-listing known bad strings is more reliable than an allow list
why: Canonicalizing before validating defeats encoded variants, and rejecting is more predictable than repairing. Block lists miss variants, the client can be bypassed, and output safety depends on context-specific encoding at output.

q: Which TWO practices reduce risk when reusing open-source libraries? (Choose two.)
opts: Pull libraries only from controlled registries, with pinned versions and verified hashes
Always update to the newest release automatically, without testing it first
Copy snippets from online forums directly into production code for speed
Prefer the library with the most downloads and skip any review of its maintenance
Keep an inventory of components and versions, and scan them for known vulnerabilities
why: Software composition analysis and an inventory find known flaws, and controlled sources with pinning and hashes prevent substitution. Popularity alone, untested automatic updates and unvetted snippets add risk.

q: Which THREE practices belong to secure session management? (Choose three.)
opts: Generate identifiers with a cryptographically secure random generator
Keep the same identifier for the life of the user account
Set the Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite cookie attributes
Put the session identifier in the URL so it survives bookmarks
Invalidate the session on the server at logout and after the timeout
why: Unpredictable identifiers, protective cookie attributes and server-side invalidation are standard. Identifiers in URLs leak through logs and referrers, and a permanent identifier makes theft and fixation worse.

q: Which TWO are benefits of tokenization compared with encrypting a sensitive field? (Choose two.)
opts: Systems that only see tokens may fall outside regulatory scope
It removes the need to protect the token vault
A stolen token has no mathematical relationship to the original value
It allows the original value to be calculated from the token with the right key
why: Tokens are surrogates, so a breach of a token-only system reveals nothing about the data and the compliance footprint shrinks. The vault becomes the high-value target, and tokens are not derived from the value with a key.

q: A time-of-check to time-of-use flaw can be avoided by checking permission and performing the action on the same handle in one atomic operation.
opts: True
False
why: The window between the check and the use is what an attacker exploits, so binding both to the same object atomically removes the gap.

q: Obfuscation of source code is a reliable way to protect an embedded secret key from an attacker with the binary.
opts: True
False
why: Obfuscation slows analysis but does not prevent extraction, so secrets belong in protected storage such as a hardware-backed keystore or a service, not in the binary.

q: A static analysis scan can show how much of the code has been exercised by the test suite.
opts: True
False
why: Static analysis reads code without executing it, and code coverage is measured by running tests. The two are separate activities even though both appear in a secure review program.

q: The first step after finding an unexpected backdoor-like function in a dependency is to keep using it and add a comment so that future maintainers are aware.
opts: True
False
why: A suspected malicious component should be investigated, its provenance checked, exposure assessed and, if confirmed, removed or replaced and incident response started.

q: A watchdog timer is an availability control that detects a hung process and triggers recovery, such as restarting it.
opts: True
False
why: Watchdogs monitor liveness, and a missed heartbeat prompts a reset or failover. They support resiliency but do not detect data tampering.

q: The CWE Top 25 ranks weakness types, and the OWASP Top 10 groups risks into categories, so a team may use both to prioritize code review.
opts: True
False
why: They are complementary lists: CWE names the types of coding mistakes, while the OWASP list groups web application risks for awareness. Neither is a complete standard.

q: A team has the full source code of a new service and wants to find flaws before it is deployed anywhere. Which testing type is the BEST starting point?
opts: Static application security testing
A distributed denial of service simulation
Dynamic application security testing against production
A bug bounty program
why: Static analysis examines code without running it, so it can start as soon as code exists and points to the exact location. Dynamic testing needs a running application, a bounty program is run on live systems, and a denial of service simulation tests resilience rather than code flaws.

q: A vendor delivered only a compiled web application running in a staging environment, with no source code. Which technique can find vulnerabilities?
opts: A code review of the branching strategy
Dynamic application security testing from the outside
Static analysis of the source code
Software composition analysis of the source repository
why: DAST interacts with a running application like an attacker and requires no source, which fits this case. Source-based techniques are not possible without the code or repository.

q: A team wants accurate findings with few false positives by observing code behavior from inside the application while functional tests run. Which technology fits?
opts: A network port scanner pointed at the application servers
Interactive testing with an instrumented agent
A web application firewall configured in blocking mode
A source line counter run against the repository on each build
why: IAST places sensors in the running application so findings are tied to actual code paths exercised by tests. A port scanner only sees network exposure, a firewall is a protective control rather than a test, and a line counter measures size.

q: A parser for a binary file format has crashed unpredictably in production after receiving unusual files. Which technique is MOST likely to find similar flaws before release?
opts: Coverage-guided fuzz testing with malformed inputs
Reviewing the user interface for accessibility problems
Scanning every dependency for outdated version numbers
Checking that the code follows the team naming conventions
why: Fuzzing generates large numbers of malformed inputs to provoke crashes and memory errors, and is especially effective on parsers. Dependency scanning, accessibility reviews and naming checks do not exercise the parser with hostile data.

q: A company hires an outside firm to attempt to break into its application. What must be in place BEFORE testing starts?
opts: A promise from the testers to fix any vulnerabilities they find
Written authorization and agreed rules of engagement for the work
Disabling all the monitoring so testers can work unobserved
Production database credentials given to the testers in advance
why: Written authorization and agreed rules protect both parties and prevent accidental damage or legal exposure by defining what is in scope. Testers do not fix flaws, disabling monitoring defeats part of what is being validated, and unneeded credentials are not a prerequisite.

q: A manager asks why the team runs both vulnerability scans and annual penetration tests. What is the BEST explanation?
opts: Scans give frequent breadth over known weaknesses; pen tests show chained exploits
They are the same activity, repeated twice to satisfy the auditors
Scans exploit the weaknesses they find, while penetration tests only list them
Penetration tests replace scans whenever the testing budget is limited
why: Automated scans are cheap and repeatable and find known issues, while penetration testing is a skilled attempt to exploit and combine flaws to demonstrate real impact. The roles in the other statements are reversed, identical or incorrectly substituted.

q: A company copies its production customer database into a test environment to make tests more realistic. What is the BEST control?
opts: Leave it unchanged, because the test network is internal
Tell the testers not to look at the personal data fields
Encrypt the test database but keep the real values inside it
Use synthetic data, or mask and anonymize the data first
why: Test environments typically have weaker controls, so real personal data must not be there unmasked. Synthetic or masked data keeps tests useful and reduces breach and compliance exposure. An internal network, verbal instructions or encryption alone do not remove the exposure.

q: A static scanner reports hundreds of findings, many of which turn out not to be real. What is the BEST response?
opts: Fix every finding in order without first checking whether it is real
Disable the tool because false positives make its results worthless
Mark every finding as accepted risk to clear the backlog quickly
Tune the rules and triage by risk instead of ignoring the tool
why: False positives are normal and are managed by tuning and triage; ignoring the tool risks false negatives from real flaws that get missed. Blanket acceptance without assessment is not a legitimate risk decision, and fixing all findings blindly wastes effort.

q: A critical vulnerability was fixed last quarter and appears again after a refactor. What practice would MOST directly prevent that?
opts: Train developers on the organization's password policy
Raise code coverage targets for modules unrelated to the fix
Move the application to a different hosting region
Add an automated regression test for that exact vulnerability
why: A regression test that exercises the exact flaw fails the build if it returns. Coverage numbers on unrelated code, password training and moving regions do not guard against reintroducing that defect.

q: Release criteria require no open critical vulnerabilities, but one remains the day before launch and the business wants to proceed. What is the appropriate action?
opts: Get documented acceptance from the accountable owner, with mitigations
Remove the vulnerability from the report so that the launch is not delayed
Have the project manager approve the exception quietly and note it in the plan
Reclassify the vulnerability as low severity so the release criteria are met
why: Releasing with a known critical flaw is a business risk decision that belongs to the accountable owner, made with full information and recorded with mitigations and a plan. Silent exceptions, reclassification and omission undermine integrity of the process.

q: A team wants to confirm that its new login feature rejects hostile behavior, such as repeated guesses, tampered tokens and skipped steps. Which testing style does this describe?
opts: Compatibility testing across browsers
Usability testing of the login page
Load testing to find the throughput limit
Negative testing based on abuse cases
why: Negative testing deliberately applies invalid and hostile input and actions to confirm that they are safely refused, often derived from abuse cases. The others test performance, usability and compatibility rather than hostile behavior.

q: Which TWO statements correctly contrast static and dynamic application security testing? (Choose two.)
opts: Static testing examines code without running it and can identify the line with the flaw
Dynamic testing probes a running application and can reveal runtime and configuration issues
Dynamic testing identifies the exact source file and line for each finding
Static testing requires a deployed environment with user traffic
why: Static testing works on code and gives locations, while dynamic testing works on the running system and finds issues visible only at runtime. The reversed statements are common mistakes.

q: Which THREE are characteristics of an effective penetration test engagement? (Choose three.)
opts: A report with findings, evidence and remediation advice
Testers who actively attempt to exploit weaknesses to show impact
Immediate public release of findings
A written scope and authorization before testing begins
Testing of any system the testers find, regardless of the scope
why: A penetration test is authorized, scoped, exploitation-oriented and ends in actionable reporting. Testing outside the agreed scope can be illegal, and findings are confidential until fixed.

q: Which TWO practices reduce the risk of using test environments? (Choose two.)
opts: Use synthetic or masked data in place of production records
Give all employees access for convenience
Keep the test systems unpatched since they are not production
Apply access control and monitoring to test systems
why: Test systems often hold copies of real data and are weakly protected, so masking data and applying access control close the gap. Open access and no patching enlarge the exposure.

q: Interactive application security testing can only observe the code paths that the tests running against the application actually exercise.
opts: True
False
why: IAST places sensors inside the running application and reports on what executes while tests run, so its coverage depends on the quality of those tests. That is why it is usually combined with other testing techniques.

q: Runtime application self-protection is primarily a testing technique that is used before release to find flaws.
opts: True
False
why: RASP embeds protection inside the running application to detect and block attacks as they happen, so it is a protective control used in production. The in-application technique used during testing is IAST.

q: A high code coverage percentage proves that the tests check security behavior correctly.
opts: True
False
why: Coverage shows which code ran during tests, not whether the tests make meaningful checks. Security test cases must also address abuse cases and error paths.

q: A penetration test that reports no critical findings proves that the application contains no exploitable vulnerabilities.
opts: True
False
why: A penetration test shows what skilled testers could achieve within the agreed scope and time. It is not a complete list of vulnerabilities and does not replace scanning, code review or design review.

q: A false negative from a security test is generally more dangerous than a false positive because it creates unwarranted confidence.
opts: True
False
why: A false positive wastes effort on an issue that is not real, but a false negative is a real flaw the test missed, so the team believes the software is safer than it is. Tuning and triage keep false positives manageable without ignoring the tool.

q: A team must justify which testing techniques to apply at which stage of a new payment product. What should the security testing strategy be derived from?
opts: The testing tools the organization already holds licenses for, because they cost nothing extra
The test plan from the previous product, copied unchanged to save the team some effort
The risk assessment, security requirements and threat model
The preferences of the testers who are available during the first sprint of the project
why: A strategy ties techniques to the risks that matter and to the stated requirements, and the plan then adds scope, environments, roles and exit criteria. Existing licenses, copied plans and tester preference are convenience, not risk-based reasoning.

q: Testers receive architecture documents, source code and administrator accounts before they start looking for vulnerabilities. Which testing approach is this?
opts: Unknown-environment testing
Known-environment testing
Black-box testing from the outside
Blind acceptance testing
why: With full knowledge of the environment, often called white-box or known-environment testing, the testers work efficiently and thoroughly. Unknown-environment (black-box) testing starts with nothing, which better reflects an external attacker but finds fewer deep issues in the same time.

q: Which scenario is the best example of nonfunctional security testing?
opts: Measuring login response time under load while throttling repeated failures
Confirming that the Forgot password link opens the correct page when clicked
Verifying that the invoice report contains the right columns in the right order
Checking that a manager can approve a purchase order within the workflow
why: Performance, reliability and scalability under attack-like conditions are nonfunctional qualities. The other options verify what the features do, which is functional behavior, including the functional security of approvals.

q: A developer reports that a component works on her machine but fails with the production message broker. Which test environment practice would have found this earlier?
opts: More unit tests that mock every outside dependency, run on the developer's machine
A review of the broker documentation by the team at the end of each sprint
A penetration test of the final release candidate shortly before launch
An environment that mirrors production, with a test harness for interoperability testing
why: Interoperability problems appear when real components talk to each other, so a production-like environment and a harness that drives the interfaces find them early. Mocked tests hide integration faults, documentation review is passive, and a late penetration test is too slow and too narrow.

q: A company publishes a vulnerability disclosure policy, runs a private bug bounty with vetted researchers and promises not to take legal action against good-faith reports. Which outline topic does this support?
opts: Attack surface validation
Cryptographic validation
Security researcher outreach
Regression testing
why: Researcher outreach channels outside skills into the product and sets expectations for reporting and fixing. The other items validate exposure, algorithms or change safety rather than manage external reporters.

q: After a release, the team compares the actual externally reachable endpoints, ports and features with the list recorded in the design. Which test objective is this?
opts: Load testing, confirming the limits of the production hardware
Usability testing, confirming that users can find the endpoints
Acceptance testing, confirming that the business signed the endpoint list
Attack surface validation, confirming the exposure matches the design
why: Validating the attack surface finds unintended exposure such as debug endpoints and leftover services. The others test capacity, ease of use or business approval and would not reveal unplanned entry points.

q: Which is the key difference between dynamic and interactive application security testing?
opts: Dynamic testing needs the source code, while interactive testing works from compiled binaries only
Interactive testing runs only before the build, while dynamic testing runs only in production
Dynamic testing identifies the line of code, while interactive testing cannot locate any flaws
Interactive testing runs an agent inside the application, dynamic testing probes from outside
why: IAST instruments the application and watches execution during tests, so findings map to code and fewer are false. DAST needs no source and cannot name the line. Neither is limited to one phase in the way the other options claim.

q: A team feeds a file parser thousands of copies of a valid sample file, each with a few randomly altered bytes. Which technique is this?
opts: Generation-based fuzzing
Regression testing
Mutation-based fuzzing
Static analysis
why: Mutation fuzzers alter existing valid inputs, whereas generation-based fuzzers build inputs from a model of the format. Regression tests rerun known cases, and static analysis does not execute the parser.

q: To confirm that an order service rolls back correctly and does not leave the system exposed when its database disappears halfway through a transaction, a tester deliberately cuts the connection. Which technique is this?
opts: Penetration testing with social engineering
Static analysis of the data layer
Fault injection, a kind of failure testing
Interface review of the logging configuration
why: Failure testing creates abnormal conditions on purpose, such as faults, resource exhaustion or dependency loss, to see whether the software fails securely and recovers. The other activities do not break the system at run time.

q: A new payment gateway generates session keys from a pseudorandom generator seeded with the system clock. What should cryptographic validation conclude?
opts: The keys are strong, because the clock changes every millisecond and the algorithm is standard
The keys are weak only if the algorithm is secret, so the design is acceptable as it stands
The keys are safe if they are encoded in Base64 before being stored in the database
The keys are predictable because the seed has little entropy
why: A strong algorithm fed with a guessable seed produces guessable output, so keys must come from a cryptographically secure generator with a good entropy source. Encoding does not add unpredictability, and secrecy of the algorithm is irrelevant.

q: A security test suite is added to the pipeline so that every commit runs unit, integration and security checks and reports within minutes. Which outline concept does this describe?
opts: Continuous testing
Acceptance testing by customers
Penetration testing by an outside firm
Disaster recovery exercises
why: Continuous testing automates verification throughout the pipeline for fast feedback. Acceptance testing, outside penetration tests and recovery drills are periodic and manual in the scenarios they usually describe.

q: A tester wants to prove that the application cannot be tricked into letting a user skip the payment step. Where should the test cases come from?
opts: The misuse and abuse cases written during requirements
The coding style guide the developers follow
The marketing description of the checkout page
The network diagram of the test environment
why: Abuse cases describe how a feature could be subverted, so they directly produce negative tests such as skipping steps. Style guides, marketing text and network diagrams do not describe adversarial behavior.

q: Documentation review finds that the installation guide tells administrators to disable the firewall during setup and leave it off, and an error message prints a database connection string. What is the best conclusion?
opts: Both are security defects and must be corrected and verified
Only the error message matters, because documentation is not part of the product
Neither matters, because installers are trusted people who will know better
Only the guide matters, because error messages are seen by too few users to matter
why: Installation, setup instructions, error messages, user guides and release notes are part of what customers rely on, and unsafe instructions or leaking messages are defects. Verifying them is a defined testing activity.

q: While reviewing a build, a tester finds an undocumented administrative URL that bypasses the login check. What should the tester do?
opts: Ignore it because it is not in the requirements and so cannot be a failure
Add it to the user guide so that it becomes documented behavior
Wait for a customer to use it before deciding whether it matters
Report it as a security defect and trace where it came from
why: Hidden functionality, whether a leftover debug feature or a backdoor, expands the attack surface and must be found, removed or properly controlled. Documenting it or waiting for customers leaves the exposure in place.

q: A scan finds a vulnerability rated high, but it can only be reached by an administrator on a segregated network. How should the test results be analyzed?
opts: Treat the score as final because the tool already knows the environment
Automatically downgrade it to informational because it is on an internal network
Block the release regardless of context so no high rating is ever shipped
Assess exploitability, exposure and impact against the release criteria
why: Results feed product and release decisions only after context is added: reachability, compensating controls, data sensitivity and the break/build criteria. A raw score and a blanket rule both ignore context, and a blanket downgrade is unjustified.

q: The team tracks defects and vulnerabilities in one tracker. Which attribute is most important for a security finding that is not shown for ordinary defects?
opts: Restricted visibility until it is fixed, plus a risk score such as CVSS
A color that matches the team's branding for each severity level
A free-text field that records the name of the tester in full
A due date that is always set to the end of the quarter
why: Vulnerability reports can help attackers if widely visible, so access should be limited, and a score and owner allow prioritization. Branding colors, tester names and an arbitrary due date add little.

q: To test a reporting feature, a team builds a synthetic data set that keeps the foreign key relationships between customers, orders and invoices, and has realistic value distributions. Which test data property are they preserving?
opts: Anonymity of real customers through direct copying of the production tables
Tokenization of the customer table
Obfuscation of the order identifiers
Referential integrity and statistical quality similar to production
why: Generated test data should behave like production data in structure and distribution so that tests are meaningful, without using real personal data. Copying is not synthetic, and the other options describe protective transformations rather than data quality.

q: A team masks production names and e-mail addresses before loading a test database, but leaves birth date, postcode and gender intact. A reviewer objects. Why?
opts: Combining the remaining fields can still identify individuals
Birth date, postcode and gender are encrypted by default in every database engine
Masking names is illegal when the remaining fields are retained for testing
The reviewer is wrong because only direct identifiers like names can reveal people
why: Quasi-identifiers can single out individuals when combined, so reuse of production data needs anonymization or aggregation controls, not just masking of obvious fields. The other statements are false.

q: An independent group that did not build the software tests it against the requirements before release. Which activity is this?
opts: Developer unit testing
Independent verification and validation
Configuration management auditing
Vulnerability disclosure handling
why: Independent verification and validation uses a team separate from development to reduce bias and strengthen assurance. Unit tests are written by the developers, and the other options are different activities.

q: A project is following an international standard that lists techniques for software testing, and is also using an open methodology manual for operational security testing. Which pair is plausible?
opts: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 and the OSSTMM methodology
ISO/IEC 27001 and the Common Vulnerability Scoring System
PCI DSS and the Software Bill of Materials specification
NIST SP 800-88 and the Common Weakness Enumeration list
why: The outline names standards from ISO, OSSTMM and the Software Engineering Institute as sources for test strategy. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 is a software testing standard, and OSSTMM is an open methodology. The other pairs are for management systems, scoring, inventories, sanitization and weakness lists.

q: A service uses synthetic transactions that log in and place a small order every minute from several regions, and alert when the sequence fails or slows. What is the main security-relevant value?
opts: Replacement of the need for any pre-release testing in the pipeline
Proof that the application has no injection flaws in any form
Early detection of broken controls or outages in production
Reduction of the attack surface of the login page itself
why: Synthetic monitoring exercises key paths continuously and reveals regressions and outages. It does not replace pre-release tests, prove the absence of flaws or shrink the surface.

q: Which TWO findings from a penetration test should be added as regression tests? (Choose two.)
opts: A discovered authorization bypass on an API endpoint, once fixed
The tester name and the date of the report
A fixed SQL injection in a search field
The cover page and table of contents of the report
why: Every fixed vulnerability should get an automated test so it cannot silently return. Report metadata such as names, dates and cover pages is not behavior that code can regress.

q: Which TWO are good practices for running a fuzzing campaign? (Choose two.)
opts: Keep the crashing inputs, triage them and add fixes with tests
Run it against production so that the findings reflect real data
Discard crashes that are hard to reproduce, since they cannot be real
