Run it in an isolated environment and monitor for crashes and hangs
why: Fuzzers can crash or corrupt what they test, so isolate them and keep crashing inputs for triage and regression. Production use is risky, and intermittent crashes often signal real memory errors.

q: Which TWO are valid reasons to run security tests in the build pipeline on every change? (Choose two.)
opts: Automated checks produce quick, repeatable feedback for the developer
Failed tests can simply be marked as passed when a deadline is near
Defects are cheaper to fix when found close to the change that introduced them
Pipeline tests make manual code review and penetration testing unnecessary
why: Frequent automated tests shorten the feedback loop and lower fix cost, but they complement human review and deeper testing. Overriding failures without approval defeats the gate.

q: Which THREE are appropriate elements of a security test plan? (Choose three.)
opts: A rule that testers may only test features that have been documented
Scope, environments and the data to be used
A promise that all defects will be hidden from the audit team
Roles, schedule and reporting of results
Entry and exit criteria, including break and build thresholds
why: A plan defines what is tested, with which data and criteria, by whom and how results are reported. Hiding defects from auditors and limiting tests to documented features both undermine the purpose.

q: Unknown-environment testing, in which testers receive no internal information, generally finds deeper internal flaws faster than known-environment testing with source code access.
opts: True
False
why: Having documentation and code lets testers reach internal flaws efficiently. Unknown-environment testing better represents an outside attacker but explores less in the same time.

q: A bug bounty program replaces the need for internal security testing.
opts: True
False
why: Bounty programs add diverse outside skills but depend on triage capacity, scope and incentives, and they find issues after release. Internal testing is still needed earlier in the lifecycle.

q: Stress testing and break testing deliberately push a system beyond normal limits to learn how it fails and whether it fails securely.
opts: True
False
why: Failure testing studies behavior under extreme load, resource exhaustion and faults, including whether security controls stay in force when the system degrades.

q: Verifying release notes and user guides is outside the scope of secure software testing because documents are not code.
opts: True
False
why: Documentation such as installation instructions, error message catalogs, user guides and release notes can instruct unsafe actions or disclose information, so its accuracy and safety are verified.

q: A fuzzer that builds inputs from a grammar of the file format is performing generation-based fuzzing.
opts: True
False
why: Generation-based fuzzers create inputs from a model of the format or protocol, while mutation-based fuzzers alter existing samples.

q: Results of a security test are interpreted only by the testers, who alone decide whether the product can be released.
opts: True
False
why: Test results inform product management and the accountable owner, who weigh impact, break/build criteria and risk acceptance. Testers report and advise but do not own the release decision.

q: A build server produces release packages that are installed by thousands of customers. Which control BEST lets customers verify that a package really came from the vendor and was not altered?
opts: Post a checksum on the same download page that serves the package
Digitally sign the artifact and publish the verification certificate
Rename the file with a random version number for each customer
Compress the package with a password that is shared by email
why: A digital signature binds the artifact to the publisher and detects tampering, and customers verify it with the published key or certificate. A checksum stored next to the file can be replaced by an attacker, and password compression and renaming do not establish origin or integrity.

q: An organization wants to limit exposure if a new version has a hidden flaw. Which deployment technique is BEST?
opts: Skipping the staging environment in order to reduce cost
A canary release to a small share of users first
Disabling monitoring until the release has settled in
Deploying to every user at once so the rollout finishes quickly
why: A canary release limits who is affected and provides the chance to detect problems and roll back before wider exposure. Full deployment, skipping staging and disabling monitoring all increase risk.

q: A review of the delivery pipeline finds that all builds use a long-lived administrator credential stored in the pipeline settings. Which change is MOST important?
opts: Store the credential in the source repository so it is always available
Rename the credential so that its administrative purpose is not obvious
Share the credential with the operations team to provide some redundancy
Use short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials issued per build
why: The pipeline is a high-value target, so credentials should be minimal, temporary and protected, limiting damage if a build is compromised. Renaming gives no protection, sharing widens exposure and storing it in the repository leaks it.

q: Three vulnerabilities are open: a CVSS 9.8 flaw in an internal tool with no network exposure, a CVSS 7.5 flaw in an internet-facing service listed in the known exploited vulnerabilities catalog, and a CVSS 5.0 flaw in a test server. Which should be addressed FIRST?
opts: The 9.8 flaw in the internal tool, because its base score is the highest
The 7.5 flaw in the internet-facing service being exploited in the wild
The 5.0 flaw in the test server, because it will be the quickest to fix
All three at the same time, in whatever order the team happens to choose
why: Prioritization should combine severity with exposure and exploitation evidence, and active exploitation of an internet-facing system makes the risk immediate. Base score alone ignores context, ease of fixing is not a risk criterion, and refusing to prioritize wastes scarce effort.

q: A vendor receives a report of a serious flaw from an outside researcher. What is the BEST first step?
opts: Require the researcher to sign an agreement that bans any future disclosure
Ignore the report until a customer complains about the same behavior
Acknowledge and validate the report, then coordinate the fix with the reporter
Publish the technical details at once so that customers can protect themselves
why: A coordinated disclosure process acknowledges, validates and fixes the issue while agreeing a timeline with the reporter. Ignoring invites public disclosure, permanent gag demands damage trust, and publishing details before a fix exposes customers.

q: A critical patch cannot be applied for two weeks because it requires a long testing cycle on a legacy system. What is the BEST interim step?
opts: Apply the patch to production without any testing in order to close it
Turn off the logging that reports the vulnerability on the system
Apply compensating controls such as virtual patching
Ignore the vulnerability and take no action until the patch is ready
why: Compensating controls reduce exposure while the patch is validated, and a documented exception keeps accountability. Ignoring it leaves the risk open, untested patches can break production, and disabling logging hides evidence.

q: A software product reaches its end-of-life date, and the vendor will stop issuing patches. Which action is MOST appropriate for a customer who depends on it?
opts: Remove its logging in order to improve the performance of the system
Continue using it indefinitely on the grounds that it still works correctly
Plan migration to a supported product and add compensating controls meanwhile
Wait until a breach occurs before beginning any planning for the change
why: Unsupported software accumulates unfixable vulnerabilities, so the right response is to plan retirement or replacement and isolate or protect the system meanwhile. Using it indefinitely, reducing logging and waiting for a breach all raise risk.

q: Retired application servers are being returned to a leasing company. They held confidential records. Which action is MOST appropriate?
opts: Format the disks with a quick format and reinstall a clean operating system
Delete the files and empty the recycle bin on each server before return
Remove the asset labels from the servers so they are not identifiable
Sanitize the media with a method suited to its sensitivity, and keep a record
why: Sanitization must make data unrecoverable in line with NIST SP 800-88, and records show it was done. Deleting files or quick formatting leaves recoverable data, and removing labels has no effect on data.

q: Which TWO are elements of a secure CI/CD pipeline? (Choose two.)
opts: Disabling build logging to save storage
A single shared administrator account for every pipeline job
Isolated, ephemeral build runners with short-lived credentials
Signed build artifacts with access-controlled and logged pipeline changes
why: Isolation and short-lived credentials limit what a compromised job can do, and signing with controlled changes protects integrity. A shared administrator account and no logs both make compromise easier and harder to detect.

q: Which TWO should be considered when prioritizing which vulnerabilities to fix first? (Choose two.)
opts: The exposure and business criticality of the affected system
Which vulnerability was found by the most senior tester
The order in which the findings appear in the report
Evidence that the vulnerability is being actively exploited
why: Risk-based prioritization uses exploitation evidence, exposure and criticality in addition to base severity. Who found a flaw and report order say nothing about risk.

q: A digital signature on a software release shows who published it and that it was not altered after signing, but not that it is free of vulnerabilities.
opts: True
False
why: A signature proves the publisher and integrity since signing. A signed artifact can still contain flaws, or malicious code if the signing process itself was compromised.

q: The CVSS Base score is the same for every organization, while environmental metrics adjust it to a specific deployment.
opts: True
False
why: The Base score captures intrinsic characteristics of the vulnerability. Threat metrics (called Temporal in version 3.1) and Environmental metrics adjust it for current exploitation and for the asset and controls in a particular organization.

q: Cryptographic erase, which destroys the key that protects encrypted data, can be an acceptable way to sanitize media when strong encryption was applied from the start.
opts: True
False
why: Without the key the encrypted data cannot be read, which NIST SP 800-88 recognizes as a sanitization technique. It works only if the data was strongly encrypted from the beginning and every copy of the key is destroyed.

q: A blue-green deployment allows a quick rollback by switching traffic back to the previous environment.
opts: True
False
why: Two identical environments are kept, so the team deploys to the idle one, switches traffic when it is ready and can switch back if a problem appears. A canary deployment instead exposes a new version to a small share of users first.

q: A team is about to move a new application from quality assurance into production. The administrators have only used the legacy platform and the privacy officer has not reviewed the data flows. Which activity should the team perform before go-live?
opts: An operational risk analysis of the environment, training and legal compliance
A cosmetic review of the production dashboards to improve the look of the charts
A rewrite of the application in a different language to match the administrator skills
A freeze on all patches for the platform until the first quarter after the launch
why: Operational risk analysis looks at the deployment environment, how well administrators and users are prepared, regulatory and privacy obligations and system integration, before the system goes live. The other options neither assess those risks nor reduce them.

q: Production servers are found to differ from the approved baseline: some have extra services, others have older libraries. Which control would have prevented this drift?
opts: A monthly meeting where administrators describe the changes they have made
A policy that discourages administrators from making configuration changes
A larger set of servers so that the differences average out across the fleet
Version-controlled baselines with automated drift detection
why: A controlled baseline stored in version control, together with automated drift detection and remediation, makes unauthorized differences visible and reversible. Verbal reporting, a discouraging policy and scale do not enforce the baseline.

q: A vendor signs its release binaries, but customers worry that a compromised build server could sign malicious output. Which practice lets independent parties confirm that the released binary matches the published source?
opts: A longer signing key, since a stronger key stops the build server from signing bad output
Reproducible builds, where the same source yields bit-for-bit identical output
A password-protected archive for the download, with the password sent separately
A second signature applied by the same build server after the build
why: A reproducible build lets independent parties rebuild from the published source and compare the result with the released binary, which detects tampering inside the build step that a signature cannot, because a compromised builder simply signs the malicious output. A longer key or a second signature from the same server adds nothing, and a password-protected archive gives no assurance about origin.

q: Application credentials are currently stored in a configuration file in the repository, with a copy on each server. Which approach is the most appropriate for storing and managing them?
opts: An encrypted configuration file in the repository whose key is stored in the same file
A secrets manager with access control, rotation and an audit trail
Environment variables set by hand on each server and documented in a wiki page
A shared document on the team drive that only the administrators know about
why: A dedicated manager centralizes access control, rotation and auditing for credentials, secrets, keys and certificates. A key stored with the file, hand-set variables and a shared document keep secrets scattered and unaudited.

q: An embedded product ships with a secure boot chain. During manufacturing, which activity is most important to the integrity of that chain?
opts: Generating, protecting and controlling access to the signing keys
Printing the firmware version on the casing of every device
Using the same signing key for every product the company has ever made
Storing the signing key on the build server for convenience in releases
why: Secure boot is only as strong as its key generation, access and management, because anyone who holds the signing key can produce firmware the device will accept. Labels do nothing, shared keys enlarge the damage of one leak, and a key on a build server is exposed.

q: An installer asks for administrator rights for the whole life of the application, opens a firewall port that is not used and leaves a sample account active. Which secure installation principle is violated?
opts: Least privilege and hardening, because it grants more access than needed
Complete mediation, because the installer does not recheck permissions on each file
Open design, because the installer behavior was not published to customers
Psychological acceptability, because the setup screens are too simple
why: Installation should leave the system hardened: only required privileges, ports and accounts. The scenario shows excess privilege, unnecessary exposure and a default account, none of which concerns mediation, openness or usability.

q: Before go-live, a low-value internal tool has two medium findings open, while the payment system has one high finding that cannot be fixed before launch. How should the approvals to operate be handled?
opts: Sign-off at a more senior level for the payment system, since authority rises with risk
Let the project manager sign off both so that approval decisions stay consistent
Have the security team sign off both, since it found the issues and knows them best
Skip sign-off for both, since neither system has a critical finding open
why: Approval to operate is a documented risk acceptance, and the authority needed rises with the size of the residual risk, so the payment system needs a more senior accountable owner than the internal tool. The project manager owns the schedule, the security team advises but does not own business risk, and a finding short of critical is not exempt from sign-off.

q: A security operations center collects application logs, infrastructure telemetry, traces and metrics, and correlates them with threat intelligence feeds. Which outline activity is this?
opts: Information security continuous monitoring with SIEM integration
Code review of the application source with manual inspection
Disaster recovery planning with restoration drills
Requirements elicitation using misuse cases
why: Continuous monitoring gathers observable data and analyzes it centrally, often in a SIEM, enriched with intelligence. The other options are development and continuity activities.

q: A new privacy law changes how long login records may be kept. Which part of continuous monitoring should have triggered a review of the application?
opts: Tracking regulation and privacy changes that alter requirements
Collecting more metrics about response times of the login page
Comparing the fuzzing coverage between two consecutive releases
Tuning the intrusion detection signatures on the perimeter firewall
why: Monitoring includes watching the legal and regulatory landscape, not only technical signals, because new obligations change retention, logging and notification requirements. The other items are technical activities unrelated to the law.

q: During an incident, an engineer finds suspicious activity on an application server. Which sequence reflects sensible handling?
opts: Wipe the server immediately, rebuild it and delete the logs to avoid confusion
Wait to see whether the activity continues before telling anyone responsible
Triage, contain, preserve evidence, remediate and find the root cause
Fix the symptom, close the ticket and skip the review since the service is back
why: Incident execution means triage, containment, forensics that preserve evidence, remediation and root cause analysis, and then improving requirements, tests and training. Wiping first destroys evidence, waiting delays response and skipping review repeats the problem.

q: A critical operating system flaw is announced, but the operations team cannot tell which servers and firmware versions are in production because the records are scattered across spreadsheets. What should come first?
opts: Build an accurate inventory with versions and patch levels under configuration control
Patch every server at once, on the assumption that all of them are affected
Buy a larger scanner license so that it covers more network addresses
Wait for an exploit to be published before treating the flaw as urgent
why: You can only patch, mitigate or roll back what you can identify, so an inventory with versions and patch levels kept under configuration control comes first. Patching blindly can break systems that are not affected, a bigger scanner still depends on knowing what exists, and waiting for an exploit gives attackers a head start.

q: A vulnerability tracking system records a new CVE that affects a component in three products. Which step comes immediately after the vulnerability is discovered and recorded?
opts: Close it because the component vendor is responsible for the fix
Publish the exploit details so customers can test their systems
Wait for a penetration test to confirm that it is present in every product
Triage it by exposure and exploitability, then assign an owner and a deadline
why: Vulnerability management tracks, triages, assigns, remediates and verifies. Closing it because a vendor is involved leaves exposure, publishing details early helps attackers, and waiting for a test delays the response.

q: A web application cannot be patched quickly, so the team places a service in front of it that blocks known attack patterns, and enables address space layout randomization and non-executable memory on the host. How are these measures best described?
opts: A permanent replacement for secure coding and design review
A compensating runtime control that makes exploitation harder
A form of data classification that labels the sensitive requests
A backup control that restores the data after an attack
why: WAF, ASLR and dynamic execution prevention reduce the chance that a flaw is exploited, which buys time, but the underlying defect remains. They do not replace correct code, classify data or restore anything.

q: A service restores from backup after a failure. Management wants the restored data to be no more than 15 minutes old and the service back within 2 hours. Which continuity design decision most directly supports the 15-minute target?
opts: Frequent replication or log shipping, at most 15 minutes behind
A warm standby site sized to carry the entire load within 2 hours
A yearly disaster recovery exercise with a written report to the board
A longer retention period for the weekly full backups of the database
why: The recovery point objective describes tolerable data loss, which is addressed by how often data is copied. A standby site and exercises relate to recovery time, and longer retention does not make backups fresher.

q: An operations team must design resilience against a distributed denial of service attack and the loss of a storage node. Which design combination is appropriate?
opts: A single high-capacity server and a manual process to restart it
Traffic scrubbing and erasure coding or replicas across sites
Blocking all traffic from foreign countries and keeping one storage copy
A longer session timeout so that users can reconnect when service resumes
why: Operational resilience uses redundancy such as replicas or erasure codes so data survives a node loss, and capacity and filtering to absorb floods. A single server, broad blocking with no redundancy and a timeout change do not address either failure.

q: A customer contract promises 99.9 percent availability per month and a four-hour response to critical vulnerability reports. How should these commitments be classified?
opts: They are recovery point objectives, which concern the age of backups
They are risk acceptance statements, signed by the supplier owner
They are functional requirements, tested through user acceptance
Service level agreements, backed by internal objectives
why: An SLA is the commitment to the customer, often with penalties, and SLOs are the internal targets that engineering tracks to meet it. RPOs, acceptance records and functional requirements are different concepts.

q: A pipeline builds a container image, runs static analysis, dependency scanning and unit tests, signs the image and deploys it only if every check passes. A developer asks to add a manual override for urgent releases. What is the best response?
opts: Allow it only as a logged, approved exception with a named approver
Allow it for everyone, because developers know when a release is urgent
Refuse it entirely, even when a critical production defect must be fixed
Allow it but remove the logging, so the exception is not slowing things down
why: Gates need an exception path that keeps accountability, which is a recorded approval by a named person and a later review. Unlimited overrides and unlogged overrides remove the control, while no path pushes teams to bypass the pipeline.

q: A deployment uses infrastructure as code. A reviewer wants the templates checked for open storage and permissive firewall rules before anything is created. Which practice is this?
opts: Running a denial of service test against the production environment
Scanning infrastructure templates in the pipeline toolchain
Rotating all passwords once the environment has been created
Archiving the templates for the retention period after decommissioning
why: Static checks of templates catch insecure provisioning before it exists, which is cheaper than finding it in production. The other options are testing or housekeeping activities that happen at other times.

q: Which TWO practices make the automated checks in a release pipeline effective as a control? (Choose two.)
opts: Letting developers re-run a failed job until the check happens to pass
Static, dependency and secret scanning on every change
A rule that anyone can edit the pipeline definition without review
Defined break criteria that fail the build, with exceptions approved by a named owner
why: Scanning on every change finds flaws early, and written break criteria with controlled exceptions turn findings into an enforced gate. Re-running a job until it passes and unreviewed pipeline edits let teams get around the gate.

q: Which TWO are correct statements about key and certificate management in operations? (Choose two.)
opts: Keys and certificates have lifecycles that need inventory, rotation, revocation and expiry monitoring
A single key can safely be used for every environment to reduce administration
Private keys are best kept in a hardware security module or managed key service
Expired certificates are only a cosmetic problem for users
why: Lifecycle management prevents outages and compromise, and protected key stores reduce theft. Expired certificates cause failures or warnings that users ignore, and shared keys across environments mean a test leak exposes production.

q: Release approval should rest on a security sign-off by the accountable owner as well as functional acceptance.
opts: True
False
why: A product may satisfy its functional requirements and still carry unacceptable residual security risk, so approval to operate is a separate decision with documented sign-off at the appropriate level.

q: Erasure coding stores data as fragments with redundancy, so the original can be rebuilt even if some fragments are lost.
opts: True
False
why: Erasure codes split data and add parity-like pieces, so loss of a node does not lose the data, which supports operational resilience with less storage than full replicas.

q: Patching should always be performed immediately in production, without testing, so that the vulnerability window is as short as possible.
opts: True
False
why: Untested patches can break production. A risk-based process tests quickly, uses an expedited path for exploited flaws and applies compensating controls while testing proceeds.

q: Information security continuous monitoring covers only technical data such as logs, and not regulatory or privacy changes.
opts: True
False
why: Monitoring in the outline includes observable data, threat intelligence, intrusion detection and response, regulation and privacy changes, and integration analysis such as a SIEM.

q: A new vulnerability is announced in a widely used logging library. What is the BEST way to find out quickly which products are affected?
opts: Wait until customers start to report problems with the products they use
Run a performance test on every product in the portfolio
Review the marketing material for each of the company's products
Query the software bill of materials inventory for the library and version
why: An SBOM is exactly the inventory that lets an organization find where a component is used and act fast. Waiting for customers, reading marketing material and running performance tests do not reveal what is inside the software.

q: An SBOM shows a component with a critical vulnerability, but the supplier states that the vulnerable function is never reachable in the product. Which artifact communicates this?
opts: A Common Criteria Protection Profile
A software escrow agreement
A penetration test report summary
A VEX statement
why: A VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) document tells consumers whether a known vulnerability actually affects a product, reducing false alarms from SBOM matching. The others are about continuity, evaluation baselines and test results, not exploitability of a specific component vulnerability.

q: A company builds software from internal packages named in a private registry. An attacker publishes a public package with the same name and a higher version number, and the build starts using it. What is this attack?
opts: Cross-site scripting
A man-in-the-middle attack on the build network
Typosquatting
Dependency confusion
why: Dependency confusion exploits package managers that prefer the highest version across registries, so a public package shadows the internal one. Typosquatting relies on misspelled names, which is not happening here, and the others are unrelated attack classes.

q: A team wants to detect newly disclosed vulnerabilities and license problems in the open-source libraries its application uses. Which tool category fits?
opts: Software composition analysis
Fuzz testing of the application input handlers
Network intrusion detection on the production segment
Static application security testing of the code the team wrote
why: SCA identifies third-party and open-source components, their versions, known vulnerabilities and licenses. SAST analyzes the code the team wrote, fuzzing sends malformed input to your code, and intrusion detection monitors network traffic.

q: A proprietary product plans to include a library under a copyleft license that requires derived works to be released under the same license. Which risk should be assessed FIRST?
opts: Usability risk arising from the quality of the library documentation
Performance risk from the additional size of the library at runtime
Licensing risk of having to release under copyleft terms
Availability risk arising from the update schedule of the library
why: Copyleft terms can oblige distributors to share source code of derivative works, which could conflict with a proprietary model, so license review comes before adoption. The other risks are real but are not the defining concern for this license type.

q: A company must buy a critical component from a new supplier. Which action provides the MOST enforceable assurance of the supplier's security practices?
opts: Choose whichever supplier offers the component at the lowest price
Put security, breach notification and audit terms in the contract
Ask the supplier to complete a short informal questionnaire by telephone
Rely on the security statements published on the supplier's marketing page
why: Contract terms are enforceable and give the buyer recourse, and a right to audit lets them verify claims. Marketing, verbal assurances and price offer no enforceable security commitment.

q: A customer needs assurance that it can keep maintaining a mission-critical custom application if the vendor goes out of business. Which arrangement addresses this?
opts: A non-disclosure agreement signed by the key vendor staff members
A longer warranty on the hardware that the application runs on
An additional penetration test carried out each year by an outside firm
Software escrow, with the deposit verified to build correctly
why: Escrow releases source code and build materials to the customer upon defined events such as insolvency, and verification confirms the deposit is usable. Hardware warranties, NDAs and penetration tests do not preserve the ability to maintain the software.

q: A buyer is comparing two products evaluated under Common Criteria, one at EAL2 and one at EAL4. What does the higher level indicate?
opts: A guarantee that the product contains no remaining vulnerabilities
Certification of the vendor to handle all classified information
More rigorous evaluation of design, testing and development processes
A larger number of security features is built into the product
why: An evaluation assurance level measures the depth and rigor of evaluation against the Security Target, not how many features the product has. No level guarantees absence of vulnerabilities, and the level is unrelated to handling classified information.

q: Which TWO are effective defenses against dependency confusion attacks? (Choose two.)
opts: Pin dependency versions with lock files and verify package hashes
Let the build tool check public registries before the private registry
Scope internal package names and resolve them only from the private registry
Always install the latest version of every package automatically
why: Controlling where internal names resolve and pinning with hashes stops substitution by a malicious higher-version package. Taking the latest version automatically and unrestricted resolution are the conditions the attack exploits.

q: An SBOM alone tells an organization whether each listed component is exploitable in the product.
opts: True
False
why: An SBOM is an inventory of components and versions. Determining exploitability requires vulnerability data and, for example, a VEX statement from the supplier.

q: Dependency pinning and verifying hashes help defend against malicious package substitution.
opts: True
False
why: Pinned versions with recorded hashes mean the build only accepts the exact artifact that was reviewed, blocking a newly published malicious look-alike or higher version.

q: A Common Criteria evaluation is performed against a Security Target, which states the security claims the evaluated product makes.
opts: True
False
why: The Security Target describes the product's security functions and the assurance claimed, and the evaluation checks those claims; a Protection Profile can capture requirements for a class of products. The evaluation assurance level then reflects how rigorous the evaluation was, not how many features exist.

q: A team selects a new open-source library for authentication. Which action best fits supply chain risk management at the identification and selection stage?
opts: Choose the one with the shortest installation instructions to reduce effort
Pick the one that the team used in the previous job without further checks
Select it based on the star count and then stop looking at it afterwards
Assess maintenance, vulnerability history, license and provenance first
why: Selection should assess the component's risk, including how well it is maintained, its history, licensing and origin, and record a treatment decision, with monitoring continuing afterward. Convenience, familiarity and popularity are not assessments.

q: An SBOM has been delivered for every release, but when a serious vulnerability in a common library was announced, the team needed two days to find the affected builds. Which weakness in the process is most likely?
opts: The SBOMs were generated in SPDX instead of CycloneDX
The SBOMs were signed with a key that is longer than necessary
The SBOMs list too few developers who maintain each internal service
The SBOMs are not in a searchable, monitored inventory
why: An SBOM is useful when it feeds an inventory that can be queried and continuously matched against vulnerability data. The format is not the problem, key length is irrelevant, and maintainers are not required elements.

q: A cloud vendor offers a SOC 2 Type II report and a completed Cloud Controls Matrix questionnaire. How should the buyer use these in analyzing the vendor?
opts: As proof that the service has no vulnerabilities, so no further assessment is needed
As a replacement for contractual security commitments and incident notification terms
As a certification that automatically extends to every other product the vendor sells
As evidence of control design and operation, after reading the scope and the period covered
why: Assessment reports show how a defined service was controlled over a period, so scope, exclusions and dates matter. They are not proof of absence of flaws, do not replace contract terms and do not cover products outside the stated scope.

q: A buyer wants evidence that a delivered firmware image is the one the supplier built, and that it has not been changed in transit. Which controls provide this?
opts: A phone call from the supplier sales representative confirming the shipment
A compressed archive with a password that is e-mailed with the download link
A digital signature and hash, with a documented chain of custody
A copy of the supplier's marketing brochure with the version number on the cover
why: Secure transfer relies on authenticity and integrity checks plus a record of who handled the item. Assurances by phone, shared passwords and brochures are not cryptographically verifiable.

q: An auditor reviewing the supplier's code repository finds that any developer can push directly to the release branch, and the build runs on a shared workstation with a long-lived administrator account. Which part of pedigree and provenance is weak?
opts: Right to audit clauses written into the supplier contract terms
End-user license agreement terms and conditions
Code repository security and build environment security
Software escrow deposit completeness and testing
why: Provenance depends on controlling who can change source and on running builds in protected, isolated environments. Contract clauses, license terms and escrow do not make the repository or build environment trustworthy.

q: A supplier objects to an on-site review of its development practices by the buyer. Which contract mechanism should have been negotiated?
opts: A larger warranty period on the delivered software
A right-to-audit clause with agreed notice and scope
A copy of the supplier source code in escrow only
A promise from the supplier to follow best practice in all of its development work
why: The right to audit lets the buyer or an independent assessor verify security claims. Warranties, escrow and general promises do not give verification access.

q: A supplier is to host a service that processes customer data and will run its own penetration tests. Which acquisition requirement best addresses the scope of testing in the shared responsibility model?
opts: An assumption that the supplier tests everything, so the buyer does not need to test
A written statement of which layers each party tests, with buyer permission
A ban on any testing by the buyer, to prevent disruption to other tenants
A requirement to test only the marketing web site of the supplier
why: The shared responsibility model divides responsibilities, so testing scope must say who tests what and what is permitted. Assuming the supplier covers everything, banning all buyer tests and testing only the brochure site leave the buyer's layers unexamined.

q: The contract with a software vendor requires that security incidents affecting the buyer be reported within 24 hours and that vulnerability notices include a coordinated fix timeline. Which element of supplier requirements is this?
opts: Vulnerability and incident notification and coordination
Maintenance and support structure, including licensing terms
Security track record, including past breaches of the supplier
Log integration into the buyer's SIEM
why: The terms define how and how fast the supplier tells the buyer and works with it on issues, which is the notification and coordination requirement. The others are different elements in the same outline objective.

q: Which supplier requirement lets a buyer detect an attack on a hosted component using its own security tooling?
opts: Delivery of the component's security logs into the buyer's SIEM in an agreed format
A supplier statement that attacks are unlikely because the product is popular
A requirement that logs be kept privately by the supplier for one year
A contract clause that forbids the buyer from using monitoring tools
why: Log integration gives the buyer visibility and correlation across its estate. Statements about popularity, supplier-only logs and a ban on monitoring all remove or prevent that visibility.

q: Which contract provision addresses who owns the code that a contractor writes specifically for the buyer, and who is liable for defects?
opts: A schedule showing when the contractor teams will attend security training
A list of the encryption algorithms used in the supplier's internal network
A statement of the supplier's preferred programming languages
Terms covering intellectual property ownership, warranty and liability
why: Contractual requirements settle ownership of intellectual property, the warranty on the delivered work and who bears liability, along with items such as escrow, EULA and SLAs. Training schedules, internal algorithms and language preferences do not.

q: A vendor release is delivered together with a statement that a listed vulnerability in an included library is not exploitable in the product because the vulnerable function is never invoked. What should the buyer do?
opts: Treat the statement as final and remove the component from the inventory
Record the VEX statement, verify it and keep monitoring the component
Reject all future vendor statements because they cannot be trusted
Delete the SBOM entry since the vulnerability does not apply
why: A VEX statement helps prioritize but is a supplier assertion, so it is tracked, checked where practical and revisited if the product changes. Removing the component from inventory or discarding the entry loses information.

q: Which TWO items should a buyer verify when assessing the origin and support of third-party software? (Choose two.)
opts: Whether support is commercial or community-based, and its end-of-life dates
The number of staff who attended the vendor's annual conference
The color scheme used in the vendor's user interface
Who develops and maintains it, and under what jurisdiction
why: Origin and support determine how quickly issues are fixed and who can compel the supplier. Interface colors and conference attendance have no bearing.

q: Which THREE are valid purposes of a software bill of materials? (Choose three.)
opts: Supporting license compliance reviews
Letting buyers see the third-party components and versions delivered
Replacing the need for supplier security assessments
Proving that every listed component is free of vulnerabilities
Identifying affected products when a component vulnerability is announced
why: An SBOM is an inventory that supports vulnerability response, license review and transparency. It says nothing about whether the components are vulnerable and does not replace assessment.

q: A supplier's SOC 2 report from three years ago for a different service is adequate evidence for a current purchase.
opts: True
False
why: Assessment reports cover a defined scope and period, so stale reports or ones for another service do not provide assurance about the service being bought.

q: Code signing is useful in a supply chain because consumers can verify the publisher and detect alteration after signing.
opts: True
False
why: A signature binds the artifact to the signer and breaks if the file changes. It does not prove the code is free of flaws, and a compromised signing process can still sign bad code.

q: Chain of custody for delivered software means documenting who held the artifact and how its authenticity and integrity were preserved during transfer.
opts: True
False
why: The record, combined with cryptographic checks, supports confidence that what arrived is what was built.

q: Software escrow guarantees that the buyer can maintain the product even if the deposit has never been tested.
opts: True
False
why: An escrow deposit has value only if it is complete and can be built, so verification of the deposit matters as much as the agreement.
